headings.text: 🌳 Decision tree: which front door does this traffic need?

notes.html:
Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request

This section is about the boxes between a client and your code, and it comes back to one question: what is this hop allowed to see, and how often does it decide? A proxy's power and its failure modes come from the same property, that it terminates and re-originates. Reading the request buys routing, retries and per-request balancing. Holding the response breaks streaming. Deciding once per connection instead of once per request leaves most of a fleet idle.

Concept map

The proxy comes first because every later box (balancer, gateway, ingress, mesh, CDN) is a reverse proxy with a particular job.

Green holds a CORE note, blue is SUPPORTING, yellow is BREADTH. 106–108 holds one CORE note (108) and two SUPPORTING; 109–111 one CORE (109) and two SUPPORTING; 112–113 one CORE (112) and one SUPPORTING. Decision tree: which front door does this traffic need?

The binding question is whether the traffic comes from the internet at all. The default leaf is one L7 load balancer: every other box has to earn its own fleet, config and failure mode. "L4 or L7?" is owned by L4 vs L7, which draws that tree.

  • API gateway (API gateway): changes if the only consumer is your own front end; then auth at the app and limits at the balancer are enough.
  • Gateway API (ingress and Gateway API): changes if an existing Ingress setup works and its controller is still maintained; ingress-nginx is not (Landscape).
  • One L7 load balancer (L7 balancing): changes if users are far away and responses are cacheable; then a CDN goes in front, and with several regions a global balancer above it.
  • Service mesh (service mesh): changes if the team can't run the control plane on call; a library or plain mTLS covers fewer services more cheaply.
  • Internal L7 balancer (L4 vs L7): changes if callers hold long-lived HTTP/2 connections; then see gRPC balancing.

Decision tree: which balancing algorithm?

The binding question is whether a key has to land on the same backend; the default leaf is plain round robin.

  • Consistent hashing (consistent hashing): changes if the per-key state can be rebuilt cheaply anywhere; then balance on load instead and accept cache misses.
  • Least request, two choices (algorithms): changes if the balancer can't count in-flight requests, as at L4; then it falls back to connection counts.
  • Weighted round robin (algorithms): changes if costs vary too; then least request with weights.
  • Round robin (algorithms): changes if one slow backend starts collecting a queue; that is the signal to move to least request.

notes.title: Proxies, Load Balancers & Gateways — Breadth Flashcards
notes.html:
Three edge defences that sit at the same hop as the CDN or the reverse proxy. Each needs a different layer of the request.

WAF

Stage: balance · per request

A web application firewall matches decrypted requests against rules for injection, traversal and known exploits, then blocks, challenges or counts. It must read the request, so it lives where TLS terminates, never on an L4 passthrough. The default that bites: AWS WAF inspects only the first 8 KB of a body behind an ALB (16 KB by default at CloudFront, up to 64 KB), and outside the console oversize handling defaults to Continue, so a payload placed after the limit is never inspected (as of Nov 2026). Run new rules in count mode before block.

DDoS protection

Stage: route · per packet

Two shapes, two defences. A volumetric or protocol flood (UDP, SYN) fills links and state tables; the answer is capacity, spreading the flood across every PoP with anycast and dropping it before it reaches you. An application-layer flood sends valid-looking requests to expensive endpoints; it needs rate limits, challenges and caching. Providers bundle the first: Cloudflare includes unmetered L3, L4 and L7 mitigation on all plans, and AWS Shield Standard covers network and transport attacks at no extra charge (as of Nov 2026). Your origin must accept traffic only from the edge, or attackers bypass it.

Bot mitigation

Stage: balance · per request

A distributed botnet sends a few requests from each of thousands of addresses, so it never trips a per-IP rate limit. Bot management scores each request instead, from TLS and HTTP fingerprints, behaviour, JavaScript checks and machine learning, then allows, challenges or blocks by score. Cloudflare's score runs from 1 (certainly automated) to 99 (certainly human), with verified bots such as search crawlers kept apart (as of Nov 2026). Like a WAF it needs the decrypted request, so it runs at the TLS-terminating edge. Expect false positives on API clients: exempt authenticated machine traffic by key, not by score.

notes.title: Forward Proxy vs Reverse Proxy — Who Chose the Hop, and What It Can See
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9110 §3.7: Intermediaries · 📜 RFC 9110 §9.3.6: CONNECT · 📜 RFC 9112 §3.2: Request target forms · nginx: ngx_http_proxy_module

TL;DR

Both are the same kind of program facing opposite ways. A forward proxy is chosen by the client and speaks for it to any server; for HTTPS it only opens a CONNECT tunnel, so it sees a host and port, not the URL. A reverse proxy is chosen by the server's owner (DNS points at it), ends the client's connection, and speaks for a set of backends the client never learns about.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:client configured with a proxyCONNECT api.vendor.com:443200blind tunnel: proxy sees host, port, SNI, bytesTLS end to end
DNS points at the proxyclient's TLS ends thereroute on Host and pathnew connection to a backendresponse returned as if from the origin

Recall

Prompt Answer
Who configures each? Forward: the client (settings, HTTPS_PROXY). Reverse: the server's owner, through DNS.
RFC 9110's name for a reverse proxy? A gateway: it acts as the origin server for the outbound connection.
What does a forward proxy see of an HTTPS request? CONNECT host:443, then SNI and byte counts. No path, no headers.
Request line a client sends to a forward proxy for http://? Absolute-form: GET http://host/path HTTP/1.1 (RFC 9112 §3.2.2).
Which headers never cross a proxy? Hop-by-hop ones: Connection and what it lists, Keep-Alive, TE, Upgrade.
Draw by hand: both proxies on one picture Client side: client → forward proxy → internet. Server side: internet → reverse proxy → pods.

The idea

Security asks the platform team to stop an AI agent from uploading files to paste sites, and suggests a rule on the egress proxy: block any URL containing /upload. The rule never fires. The agent calls https://paste.example/upload, so its HTTP client sends CONNECT paste.example:443 and then TLS bytes the proxy can't read. The path exists only inside the tunnel.

Inbound, the same team's app logs every request as coming from 10.0.3.17: their own reverse proxy, which opened a new connection. The real client is only in a header the proxy added.

One cause behind both: the client chose the forward proxy, so it sees where traffic goes but not what. The site chose the reverse proxy, which holds the certificate and sees everything, while the backend sees only the proxy.

The trade: a proxy gives one place for policy, logging and caching, and you pay with a hop on every cold connection, a component that can take all traffic down, and an identity (the client's address, the site's certificate) that now lives in that hop.

How it works

One picture, two directions; yellow hops are proxies, purple is what you don't run.

The forward proxy hides the client; the reverse proxy hides the servers.

Rule What actually happens
Who chose it RFC 9110 §3.7: a proxy is chosen by the client, a gateway acts as the origin. An interception ("transparent") proxy is chosen by neither and redirects packets.
Request line To a forward proxy, http:// goes in absolute-form and https:// as CONNECT host:port. A reverse proxy receives origin-form (GET /path) like any server.
HTTPS CONNECT turns the forward proxy into a blind relay after 2xx. The reverse proxy holds the certificate and terminates TLS.
Headers Both drop hop-by-hop fields (RFC 9110 §7.6.1), so Upgrade needs explicit handling. A forward proxy MUST add Via; a reverse proxy appends the peer to X-Forwarded-For, trusted only from the right.
The middle Each side opens its own connection, so the next hop sees the proxy's address and ports, and timeouts stack.

The tunnel costs a round trip to the proxy before TLS can start:

With r the client-to-proxy RTT and R the proxy-to-origin RTT, and the proxy on the path:

direct cold = TCP + TLS 1.3 = 2·(r + R)          ← client↔origin RTT is r + R
via proxy   = r (TCP) + (r + R) (CONNECT) + (r + R) (TLS) = 3r + 2R
extra       = r per cold connection               ← nothing once the connection is reused
r = 70 ms (proxy in another region) → +70 ms on every cold call   ← an input, not a measurement

So a central egress proxy belongs in each region, and clients should reuse connections through it.

Evolution

Lineage:2000 CONNECT specified (RFC 2817)2014 Forwarded header (RFC 7239)2022 RFC 9110 names the gateway "a.k.a. reverse proxy"2022 CONNECT-UDP (RFC 9298)2023 CONNECT-IP (RFC 9484)
  • Maturity today: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026). The definitions are unchanged since HTTP/1.1. What moves is product defaults: nginx 1.29.7 (24 Mar 2026) made HTTP/1.1 and upstream keepalive the proxy default, replacing HTTP/1.0.
  • Changed in RFC 9298 and 9484: a forward proxy can now tunnel UDP and IP over HTTP, so QUIC can go through it. A proxy that only knows TCP CONNECT forces HTTP/3 clients back to TCP.
  • What's next and what won't change: AI-agent egress brings forward proxies back into designs. Who chose the hop, and so what it sees, stays the dividing line.

On the wire

Annotated config for both directions (illustrative names).

# reverse: api.example.com resolves to this box; clients never learn a backend exists
server {
  listen 443 ssl;                        # the client's TLS ends here
  server_name api.example.com;
  location / {
    proxy_pass http://app_pool;          # a new connection inbound, origin-form request line
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;  # append the peer it saw
    # proxy_http_version: 1.1 by default since nginx 1.29.7; older builds sent 1.0 and no keepalive
  }
}

The forward side is client configuration; the server is never told.

export HTTPS_PROXY=http://egress.internal:3128   # read by curl and most HTTP client libraries
curl https://api.vendor.com/v1/models           # → CONNECT api.vendor.com:443, then TLS in the tunnel

Break it: an egress proxy of ours on 127.0.0.1 logs the request line it receives. The client fetches the same URL twice, once as a plain proxied request and once through a tunnel (-p), which is what every https:// request does.

curl -x http://127.0.0.1:$PROXY    http://127.0.0.1:$ORIGIN/reports/q3-salaries
curl -p -x http://127.0.0.1:$PROXY http://127.0.0.1:$ORIGIN/reports/q3-salaries
# proxy log, run 1: GET http://127.0.0.1:62669/reports/q3-salaries HTTP/1.1
# proxy log, run 2: CONNECT 127.0.0.1:62669 HTTP/1.1
# look for: the path is missing from the proxy's view in run 2, though both runs got the report
# naive belief predicts: the egress proxy can filter on the URL path either way

Run on Python 3.15.0 and curl 8.7.1, 22 Nov 2026: both got the body, only the first exposed the path.

Measure it

  • See it: curl -v -x http://proxy:3128 https://host/ shows CONNECT host:443 and 200 Connection established before the TLS lines; curl -v https://site/ shows the reverse proxy's certificate, never a backend's.
  • In production: forward, per destination host: CONNECT denials, open tunnels against the file-descriptor limit, tunnel setup time. Reverse, per request: nginx $upstream_response_time beside $request_time; a widening gap is the proxy, not the app.
  • Bounded by: a single egress proxy failing → all outbound calls fail → replicas per zone and a clear fail-open or fail-closed rule. Port exhaustion on the proxy → upstream connection reuse (ephemeral range).

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Same software, opposite owner. The client picks a forward proxy, which reaches any server for it. For HTTPS it only tunnels with CONNECT, so it sees host and port, not the URL. The site picks a reverse proxy through DNS. It holds the certificate, ends the connection, sees everything and fronts backends the client never learns about. Mixing them up is how teams write egress rules that can't fire.

Q · Mechanism — If both are nginx, what differs on the wire? The first line of the request. A forward proxy receives GET http://host/path in absolute-form, or CONNECT host:443 for HTTPS, and must open a connection to whatever host is named. A reverse proxy receives GET /path with a Host header and maps it to backends it already knows. After a 2xx to CONNECT the forward proxy stops parsing and relays bytes. The reverse proxy parses every request, because routing, caching and header rewriting all need it.

Q · Trade-off — An agent in your cluster calls arbitrary tool APIs. Egress proxy, or per-service network rules? Network rules match IP ranges, and SaaS APIs sit behind shared, changing CDN addresses, so a hostname allow-list needs a proxy reading CONNECT and SNI. It also logs every destination the agent touched. You pay a mandatory hop, a connection-table limit, and r per cold connection. Pick the proxy once destinations are named by hostname or need an audit trail. A few fixed partner IPs need only rules.

Q · Failure — 5,000 pods share one egress proxy and new outbound calls start failing. What ran out? Source ports on the proxy's outbound side, before CPU. Each tunnel to one destination uses one port from the proxy's address. The ephemeral range note derives about 470 new connections a second per destination on default Linux, because TIME_WAIT holds closed ports. It shows as EADDRNOTAVAIL in the proxy's log while the pods see connect timeouts. Fix: client keepalive through the proxy, more source addresses, or more proxy replicas.

Q · Design — A multi-tenant AI product streams answers to users and calls third-party tools. Where do the proxies go? Inbound, a reverse proxy per region terminates TLS and routes by path, with buffering off on the streaming route (buffering vs streaming). Outbound, tool calls leave through a per-region forward proxy holding the hostname allow-list and per-tenant audit log. Separate fleets: one faces untrusted clients, the other carries your credentials. First signal: tunnel setup time on the egress proxy. The wider design is in AI system design.

Compare

Variant Chosen by Sees HTTPS content? Typical job When you'd pick it
Forward proxy the client no, unless it decrypts with a trusted CA egress allow-lists, audit, shared cache outbound policy by hostname
Reverse proxy (gateway) the site owner yes, it holds the certificate TLS, routing, caching, balancing in front of every web service
Interception proxy neither; packets redirected no, unless clients trust its CA captive portals, corporate filtering only where clients can't be configured

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Extra latency per cold tunnelled connection r, the client-to-proxy RTT zero once reused derived (above)
When tunnel mode starts right after any 2xx to CONNECT data after that is from the origin spec: RFC 9110 §9.3.6
Default port for CONNECT none the client MUST send one spec: RFC 9110 §9.3.6
nginx upstream HTTP version 1.1 since 1.29.7; 1.0 before keepalive to backends now on by default default (as of Nov 2026): nginx docs and CHANGES
New connections per destination, one proxy IP ≈ 470/s on default Linux 28,232 ports ÷ 60 s TIME_WAIT derived in ephemeral range

Pitfalls

  • Not the same: forward proxy vs reverse proxy
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: the same binary (nginx, Envoy, Squid) can play either role, and both "sit in the middle".
    ↳ Difference: who chose the hop. The client configures a forward proxy for any destination; DNS sends every client to a reverse proxy for one site.
    ↳ Think instead: ask who would have to change a setting to remove it. The client's settings: forward. The site's DNS: reverse.
  • "The egress proxy can filter by URL"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: proxy rule languages accept URL patterns, and they work on plain http://.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: https:// goes through CONNECT host:443, and after the 200 the proxy relays encrypted bytes; the Break it shows the path vanish.
    ↳ Think instead: without decryption, a forward proxy filters on host, port and SNI only. Path rules need TLS inspection and a CA every client trusts.
  • "A reverse proxy passes every header through"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the backend sees the client's cookies and custom headers, so it seems transparent.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: hop-by-hop fields are consumed per connection (RFC 9110 §7.6.1). Upgrade and Connection never reach the backend unless configured, so the WebSocket upgrade fails there.
    ↳ Think instead: each hop is a new connection with its own hop-by-hop headers; forward the upgrade explicitly.
  • Don't run one central egress proxy for every region.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: one allow-list, one log, one fleet to patch.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every cold outbound connection pays the cross-region RTT to the proxy once more, and one outage cuts all egress.
    ↳ Do instead: a proxy per region from shared config, with connection reuse so the extra r is paid rarely.
  • Don't add an egress proxy when IP rules would do.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a proxy feels like the serious answer to "control outbound traffic".
    ↳ What goes wrong: a new hop, port and descriptor limits, and stacked timeouts, for destinations a firewall rule could name.
    ↳ Do instead: use security-group or firewall rules for a few fixed IP ranges; add a proxy once policy is per hostname or needs an audit log.
  • Shelf life: the definitions and CONNECT are durable. Proxy defaults change: nginx's upstream default moved to HTTP/1.1 in March 2026.

Connections

Path:L4 vs L7forward vs reverse proxyreverse proxy responsibilitiesL4 vs L7 balancing
  • Builds on HTTP/1.0 vs 1.1: Host and persistent connections are what a reverse proxy routes and reuses.
  • Used by API gateway: a reverse proxy that also knows the caller's identity.
  • Owned elsewhere: termination models owns where TLS ends; headers owns X-Forwarded-For trust.
  • Bounded by the ephemeral range: the proxy is a client too, and runs out of ports first.
  • Decided in AI system design: where inbound and egress proxies sit for an agent product.

notes.title: Reverse Proxy Responsibilities — The Request Pipeline and the Defaults That Bite
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9110 §7.6: Message forwarding · nginx: ngx_http_proxy_module · nginx: ngx_http_gzip_module · nginx: CHANGES · Envoy: Life of a request

TL;DR

A reverse proxy runs a fixed pipeline on every request: end TLS, pick a route, admit or reject, try the cache, rewrite headers, reuse an upstream connection. On the way back it rewrites, compresses and buffers. Each stage needs what the one before produced, so the order is forced. The bugs live in its defaults: the Host it sends, the timeout it counts, the compression it skips.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:TLS endsroute on Host + pathlimits and size checkscache lookupset Host, X-Forwarded-*pooled upstream connectionresponse: rewrite, compress, bufferaccess log with upstream timing

Recall

Prompt Answer
Host nginx sends upstream by default? $proxy_host, the name in proxy_pass, not the client's Host.
What does proxy_read_timeout 60s measure? The gap between two reads from upstream, not the whole response. Fires as 504.
Proxied requests per worker at nginx defaults? 256: worker_connections 512 counts both the client and upstream sockets.
Does nginx gzip a response for a request that came via a CDN? Not by default: gzip_proxied off skips requests carrying Via.
Upstream keepalive in nginx 1.30? On by default, with HTTP/1.1, since 1.29.7. Older builds sent HTTP/1.0.
Draw by hand: the request pipeline TLS → route → admit → cache → rewrite → upstream; back: rewrite → compress → buffer.

The idea

A team moves an orders API behind nginx. Creating an order returns 201 with "self": "http://app_pool/orders/42", and the mobile client follows a link that resolves nowhere. Nothing errored. nginx sent Host: app_pool, its default, and the app built the link from the Host it saw. The app also wrote http://, because TLS ended at the proxy and the app saw plain HTTP.

Two lines fix it: proxy_set_header Host $host and X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme. The lesson is wider. Once a reverse proxy is in front, the app learns about the client only through what the proxy chooses to tell it: the address in X-Forwarded-For, the scheme, the host. The proxy also decides the timeouts, the connection reuse and the compression that the app used to own.

The trade: one hop takes TLS, routing, admission, caching and compression off every service, and you pay with a pipeline whose defaults silently change what the app sees and when requests fail.

How it works

Request stages run top to bottom, response stages bottom to top; any stage can answer early.

A request rejected by admission or answered by the cache never costs an upstream connection, which is why those stages come first.

Rule What actually happens
Order TLS must end before the path is visible, the route before per-route limits, and private responses need identity before the cache (keys in HTTP caching).
What the app sees The proxy opens a new connection, so the peer address is the proxy's. The client's address, scheme and host arrive only as headers the proxy sets (trust them from the right).
Upstream connections Reuse avoids a TCP handshake per request and saves the proxy's source ports. nginx 1.29.7 made upstream keepalive and HTTP/1.1 the default.
Compression Do it once, at the outermost hop that sees the bytes. nginx compresses only text/html by default, and skips requests carrying Via unless gzip_proxied says otherwise.
Response buffering On by default, right for documents and wrong for token streams, which buffering vs streaming owns.

Each proxied request holds two sockets, and nginx counts both:

worker_connections = 512 (default)    ← counts client and upstream sockets
proxied requests per worker = 512 ÷ 2 = 256
long-lived streams: 50,000 ÷ 256 ≈ 196 workers at default ← raise it, and the fd limit with it

Evolution

Lineage:1999 hop-by-hop headers and proxy caching (RFC 2616)2014 Forwarded (RFC 7239)2022 RFC 9110 and 9111 restate forwarding and caching2026 nginx 1.29.7 makes upstream keepalive the default
  • Maturity today: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026). The stages are the same in nginx, Envoy, HAProxy and managed balancers; only the defaults and config syntax differ.
  • Changed in nginx 1.29.7 (24 Mar 2026), now in the 1.30 stable line: proxy_http_version defaults to 1.1, keepalive in an upstream block is on by default, and Connection isn't sent upstream by default. Configs written for older builds carry two lines that are now redundant.
  • What's next and what won't change: more of the pipeline moves into managed edges and Gateway API resources. The forced order and the app learning about the client only from headers stay.

On the wire

An annotated server block; every non-default line is there because a default bites.

upstream app_pool { server 10.0.1.10:8080; server 10.0.1.11:8080; }  # keepalive on by default since 1.29.7
server {
  listen 443 ssl;                                # TLS ends here, so the app sees plain HTTP
  server_name api.example.com;
  location /v1/ {
    proxy_pass http://app_pool;
    proxy_set_header Host $host;                 # default is $proxy_host: the app would see "app_pool"
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;  # the only way the app learns it was HTTPS
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;  # append the peer, never replace
    proxy_read_timeout 30s;                      # default 60 s, measured between reads, not in total
    gzip on;
    gzip_types application/json;                 # default list is text/html only
    gzip_proxied any;                            # default off: skips requests that arrive via a CDN
  }
}

Break it: a small reverse proxy of ours on 127.0.0.1 in front of an app that returns a self link built from Host and X-Forwarded-Proto. Mode one models nginx's default Host; mode two sets the client's host and scheme.

python3 host_rewrite.py   # client sends Host: api.example.com to the proxy both times
# default {"self": "http://127.0.0.1:62705/orders/42"}
# fixed   {"self": "https://api.example.com/orders/42"}
# look for: the upstream's address and http:// inside the app's response body
# naive belief predicts: the app sees the Host and scheme the client used

Run on Python 3.15.0, 22 Nov 2026; the proxy is a model, not nginx. nginx's proxy_redirect default would repair a Location header, but not a link in the body, a cookie domain or an OAuth callback URL.

Measure it

  • See it: curl -sv https://api.example.com/v1/x shows the proxy's certificate; an echo endpoint behind it shows the Host, X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-For the app actually received.
  • In production: per request, $upstream_response_time against $request_time, upstream connects per request (near zero when reuse works), cache hit ratio, active connections as a share of worker_connections.
  • Bounded by: a slow upstream holding every worker slot → proxy_read_timeout and a per-route connection cap. A stampede of misses → cache locking. A wrong scheme or host → explicit Host and X-Forwarded-Proto lines in every location.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A reverse proxy runs one pipeline: end TLS, route on host and path, admit or reject, try the cache, rewrite headers, send on a pooled connection; on the way back, rewrite, compress, buffer. The order is forced, because each stage needs the previous one's output and rejected or cached requests shouldn't cost a backend. The traps are defaults: nginx sends the upstream's name as Host, and its read timeout counts gaps, not totals.

Q · Mechanism — Walk a request through the proxy, in order, and say why that order. TLS ends first, because nothing after it is readable before. Routing comes next, because limits, caching and upstream choice are per route. Admission (rate limits, body size, auth where the edge does it) runs before the cache when responses are private, so a cached answer isn't served to the wrong caller. A miss gets its headers rewritten and goes upstream on a pooled connection. The response runs the same idea backwards: rewrite headers, then compress, then buffer, then log both timings.

Q · Trade-off — Compression, auth, retries: at the proxy or in the app? At the proxy when the work is the same for every service and the proxy sees the bytes first: TLS, compression once at the outermost hop, coarse limits, retries of idempotent requests on connect failure. In the app when it needs domain knowledge: per-tenant authorisation, retries of non-idempotent calls with idempotency keys, caching of anything personal. The tipping point is the second service that needs the same rule. Before that a proxy rule is config nobody owns, and after it, code repeated in each service.

Q · Failure — 50,000 SSE streams through one nginx tier. What runs out first? Worker connections and file descriptors, long before CPU. Each stream holds a client socket and an upstream socket, and worker_connections counts both, so the default 512 allows 256 per worker. Past the limit new clients fail while existing streams are fine, so it shows as a cliff, not a slope. Confirm with active connections against workers × worker_connections. Fix: raise worker_connections and worker_rlimit_nofile together, and alert at a share of the ceiling.

Q · Design — A Kubernetes product has a CDN, an ingress and a gateway. Where does each responsibility go? The binding constraint is that each stage belongs at the outermost hop that has the information it needs. The CDN takes public caching, compression and volumetric limits. The ingress ends TLS for the cluster and routes by host and path. The gateway behind it holds identity, so per-tenant quotas and auth go there (API gateway). The app keeps domain rules. First signal I'd watch: the upstream share of $request_time at each hop. Pattern context: communication patterns.

Compare

Concern At the edge (CDN) At the cluster proxy In the app When you'd pick the proxy
TLS yes, for public traffic yes, for the cluster rarely always, unless payloads must stay opaque
Caching public, shared short-lived, per route personal data a hot read path with a short TTL
Compression if it sees the bytes if nothing outside does never twice no CDN, or the CDN passes through
Rate limits by IP, volumetric by route by tenant, after auth coarse protection before the app

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
worker_connections 512 counts client and upstream sockets default (as of Nov 2026): nginx core docs
Proxied requests per worker 256 512 ÷ 2 sockets derived
proxy_read_timeout 60 s between two reads from upstream default (as of Nov 2026): nginx docs
proxy_buffers 8 × one memory page (4 KB or 8 KB) per connection default (as of Nov 2026): nginx docs
gzip_types / gzip_proxied text/html / off JSON and via-CDN requests go uncompressed default (as of Nov 2026): nginx gzip docs
Upstream Host $proxy_host the name in proxy_pass default (as of Nov 2026): nginx docs

Pitfalls

  • "The app sees the request the client sent"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: paths, query strings and cookies arrive unchanged, so the proxy looks transparent.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the peer address, the scheme and, by nginx default, the Host all belong to the proxy; the Break it returns an internal address in a link.
    ↳ Think instead: the app knows the client only through headers the proxy sets, so set Host, X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-For explicitly.
  • Not the same: proxy_read_timeout vs a request deadline
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "the proxy's timeout", and both end in 504.
    ↳ Difference: nginx's timer resets on every read, so a response trickling a byte every 50 s never times out. A deadline caps the total.
    ↳ Think instead: the read timeout catches a silent upstream; a total budget needs the app or the timeout hierarchy.
  • "gzip on compresses my JSON API"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the directive reads like a switch for all responses.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: gzip_types defaults to text/html, and gzip_proxied off skips any request carrying Via, which is every request from a CDN.
    ↳ Think instead: name the types, and decide which single hop compresses. Check with curl -H 'Accept-Encoding: gzip' -I.
  • "Upstream keepalive needs proxy_http_version 1.1 and Connection \"\""
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it was true for years, and most configs and answers online still carry both lines.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: since nginx 1.29.7, now in 1.30 stable, HTTP/1.1 and upstream keepalive are the default.
    ↳ Think instead: check the version before copying the fix; the two lines are still needed on older builds and harmless on new ones.
  • Don't add a separate proxy tier when the load balancer or ingress already does the job.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: "put nginx in front" is the reflex for TLS, routing and headers.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a managed L7 balancer or ingress usually ends TLS and routes already, so another hop adds latency, a failure point and a second set of defaults.
    ↳ Do instead: list the stages you need and add a hop only for one nothing else on the path can do.
  • Shelf life: the forced order and the header rules are durable. nginx defaults changed in March 2026; re-check them on every major upgrade.

Connections

Path:forward vs reverse proxyreverse proxy responsibilitiesbuffering vs streamingAPI gateway
  • Builds on forward vs reverse proxy: why the app sees the proxy, not the client.
  • Owned elsewhere: termination models owns where TLS ends; HTTP caching owns cache keys; rate limiting owns the algorithms.
  • Bounded by connection pooling: upstream reuse is what keeps ports and handshakes in check.
  • Used by API gateway: the same pipeline plus identity.
  • Decided in communication patterns: where gateway and proxy concerns sit in a service design.

notes.title: L4 Load Balancing — Flow Hashing, Pass-Through vs Proxy, and the Client IP
notes.html:
References

AWS: How Network Load Balancers work · AWS: NLB target group attributes · 📜 HAProxy: The PROXY protocol, v1 and v2 · nginx: ngx_stream_proxy_module

TL;DR

An L4 balancer hashes a new flow's addresses and ports, writes the pick into a flow table, and forwards every later packet of that flow by lookup. It never reads the payload. Two things decide how it behaves: whether it forwards packets (the client IP survives) or opens its own connection (it doesn't, unless the PROXY protocol carries it), and how many flows there are to spread.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:first packethash protocol, IPs, portsflow-table entrylater packets: lookup, not hashidle past the timeoutentry droppednext packet gets RST

Recall

Prompt Answer
NLB, IP targets, TCP listener: does the backend see the client IP? Not by default (as of Nov 2026); enable preserve_client_ip or PROXY protocol v2.
What happens to a flow idle past the NLB timeout? The entry is dropped; the next packet from either side gets RST.
20 connections hashed onto 20 backends: how many backends sit idle? About 36%, since (1 − 1/n)^c ≈ 1/e.

The idea

You put an L4 proxy in front of an API that rate-limits per client IP. Within an hour every client shares one bucket: the proxy opened a second TCP connection, and the source address on it is its own.

A pass-through balancer keeps the address, because it forwards the client's packets instead of making new ones. A proxy can pass it on by writing a PROXY protocol header before the first request byte.

The trade: an L4 hop costs one hash per flow and leaves the payload alone, and you pay with a backend that may not know who the client is and with balancing that's only as even as the number of flows.

How it works

Two kinds of L4 box, and what the backend's socket reports in each.

A proxy holds two sockets per client; pass-through, one table entry.

Rule What actually happens
The hash NLB hashes protocol, both IPs and ports, and the TCP sequence number, so one client's connections can land on different targets (as of Nov 2026).
The pin The pick lasts for the connection's life. Every request it carries goes to one backend, which is why HTTP/2 and gRPC pin.
The idle timer NLB tracks a TCP flow for 350 s of silence by default (60–6,000 s); UDP flows get a fixed 120 s. Keepalives reset it.

How even the spread is depends on the number of flows, not on the algorithm's name:

P(backend gets no flow) = (1 − 1/n)^c     ← each of c flows hashes to one of n backends
n = c = 20 → 0.95^20 ≈ 0.358 ≈ 1/e        ← a third of the fleet idle
round robin, c ≥ n → 0 idle               ← only a hash leaves holes, but neither spreads requests
c = 100·n → max ≈ 1.2 × mean              ← many flows: even enough

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): Linux IPVS, cloud NLBs and Google's Maglev (NSDI 2016) are all flow-hash forwarders.
  • Changed recently: NLB listeners take QUIC; kube-proxy's IPVS mode is deprecated since Kubernetes v1.35, in favour of iptables and nftables.
  • What won't change: one decision per flow, so the spread is bounded by the flow count.

On the wire

Our L4 forwarder on 127.0.0.1 (Python 3.15, 22 Nov 2026), plain, then prepending a PROXY v1 line; the backend prints its peer and first line.

client: local port 62714  proxy_protocol=False
backend: socket peer=127.0.0.1:62715  first line='GET / HTTP/1.1'
# ↑ peer port 62715 is the forwarder's own connection: the client's 62714 is gone
client: local port 62717  proxy_protocol=True
backend: socket peer=127.0.0.1:62718  first line='PROXY TCP4 127.0.0.1 127.0.0.1 62717 62716'
# ↑ source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port: the client's port is back

On localhost every address is 127.0.0.1, so the ports carry the proof.

Break it: a model, not a measurement: hash 20 long-lived connections onto 20 backends, 2,000 trials.

for _ in range(c): load[r.randrange(n)] += 1      # a flow hash looks random per connection
# look for: idle backends and the busiest one's load against the mean
# naive belief predicts: one connection per backend, nothing idle

Run on Python 3.15: 36.0% of backends idle, the busiest at 3.25× the mean; at 2,000 connections, none idle and 1.19×.

Measure it

  • See it: ss -tn on a backend (Linux): client addresses behind pass-through, one proxy address behind a proxy; per-target new-flow counts roughly equal.
  • In production: per target, active flows; NLB TCP_ELB_Reset_Count rising after quiet periods means flows outlived the idle timer.
  • Bounded by: uneven placement → many flows, or per-request balancing at L7; lost client IP → preserve_client_ip or PROXY protocol v2, accepted only from the balancer's addresses.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: An L4 balancer picks a backend per flow from addresses and ports and forwards later packets by lookup, never reading the payload. A pass-through box keeps the client's IP; a proxy opens its own connection and needs the PROXY protocol to pass it on. Its spread is only as even as its flow count: 20 connections on 20 backends leave about a third idle.

Q · Mechanism — How does a pass-through balancer let the backend answer the client directly? It rewrites or encapsulates the destination of the client's packets without terminating TCP, so the backend completes the handshake with the client's real address. With direct server return, replies leave the backend from the shared virtual IP straight to the client, and the balancer sees only the inbound half. You get throughput and the source IP, and lose any view of the response: no status, no timing, no retry.

Q · Trade-off — Pass-through or an L4 proxy? Pass-through for the client IP on the socket, the highest packet rate and no second connection. A proxy to absorb slow clients, present one egress address to a partner's allow-list, or terminate TLS at L4; it costs two sockets per client and the source IP, which PROXY protocol v2 restores.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
NLB TCP idle timeout 350 s, settable 60–6,000 s then RST on the next packet default (as of Nov 2026): AWS NLB docs
NLB UDP idle timeout 120 s, fixed the next packet is a new flow, possibly a new target default (as of Nov 2026): AWS NLB docs
Idle backends, c = n = 20 35.8% (1 − 1/n)^c derived

Pitfalls

  • "An NLB always preserves the client IP"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it does for instance targets and for UDP, and the docs lead with it.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: for IP-type target groups on TCP or TLS, preservation is off by default (as of Nov 2026), so backends see the NLB's private address.
    ↳ Think instead: check the target type and listener protocol, then enable preserve_client_ip or PROXY protocol v2 deliberately.
  • Not the same: pass-through vs an L4 proxy
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "L4 load balancers" and both ignore the payload.
    ↳ Difference: pass-through forwards the client's packets, so the backend terminates TCP and sees the client; a proxy terminates TCP and opens a second connection.
    ↳ Think instead: ask who completes the handshake with the client.
  • "A hash spreads 20 connections across 20 backends"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a good hash is uniform, so "even" sounds guaranteed.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: uniform per flow isn't even across few flows: the model left 36% idle and one at 3.25×.
    ↳ Think instead: evenness needs many flows per backend, or a per-request decision.
  • Don't raise the idle timeout to keep quiet connections alive.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: long-lived sockets get RST after 350 s, and the setting goes to 6,000.
    ↳ What goes wrong: above 350 s the target ENI's connection-tracking timeout must match too, or flows still die.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler fix: TCP or application keepalives shorter than the timer.
  • Shelf life: flow hashing and the skew arithmetic are durable; NLB defaults, listener protocols and kube-proxy modes move.

Connections

Path:reverse proxy responsibilitiesL4 load balancingL7 load balancingthe tradeoff table
  • Builds on L4 vs L7: connection or request as the unit of decision.
  • Owned elsewhere: algorithms own the choice functions; health checks own check depth.
  • Breaks when combined with HTTP/2 and gRPC: one connection, every call on one pod.
  • Bounded by keepalives and idle timeouts: what keeps a quiet flow in the table.

notes.title: L7 Load Balancing — Per-Request Picks, Upstream Pools, Routing Rules and Retries
notes.html:
References

AWS: ALB target groups (protocol version) · AWS: ALB listener rule conditions · nginx: ngx_http_proxy_module · Envoy: HTTP routing and retry semantics

TL;DR

An L7 balancer ends the client's TCP and TLS, parses each request, matches a route on host, path, header or method, and picks a backend per request, writing onto connections from its own upstream pool. That's what makes routing, least-request balancing, retries on another backend and per-route status codes possible. The defaults decide the rest: ALB talks HTTP/1.1 to targets, and nginx retries only failures that happen before a response, never a sent POST.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:TLS ends at the proxyparse requestmatch route rulepick a target for this requestreuse a pooled upstream connectionfails before a response: next target, if idempotentstatus to client

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does ALB speak to targets by default? HTTP/1.1, whatever the client used; HTTP/2 or gRPC per target group.
nginx's default proxy_next_upstream? error timeout; a sent POST or PATCH is never retried unless non_idempotent.
Envoy retries with no retry_policy? None. With a policy, num_retries defaults to 1.

The idea

A mobile app holds one HTTP/2 connection for a whole session and sends 300 requests on it. Behind an L4 box, all 300 go to whichever pod got the connection, and adding pods does nothing for that user.

An L7 proxy ends that connection itself. Each request is parsed, matched against the route table and handed to a target chosen for it, on an upstream connection the proxy already holds. One client's requests spread over every pod, and a request refused by one pod can go to another.

The trade: a decision per request buys routing, even spread and retries, and costs a TLS termination, a parse of every request, and a hop whose defaults (protocol to targets, retry rules, timeouts) now shape your traffic.

How it works

One client connection, three requests, one retry rule.

The GET never reached a backend, so retrying was safe; the POST did, so nobody knows whether it ran.

Rule What actually happens
Route rules ALB matches host, header, method, path, query string and source IP (as of Nov 2026), as Envoy and nginx do. Only a parsed request has them.
Upstream pool The proxy keeps its own connections to targets, so the backend sees the proxy's address and reads the client's from X-Forwarded-For, which reverse proxy responsibilities own.
Protocol to targets ALB sends HTTP/1.1 by default: an HTTP/2 client's streams become separate upstream requests. Target group version HTTP/2 rejects HTTP/1.1 clients; gRPC needs the gRPC version.
Retries nginx tries the next server on error or timeout by default, with no limit on tries (proxy_next_upstream_tries 0). Envoy retries only under a route's retry_policy, all within the route timeout.
The choice function Round robin by default on ALB, with least outstanding requests and weighted random as options; algorithms own them.

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): every cloud, Envoy, nginx and HAProxy ship per-request balancing; meshes put it in every pod.
  • Changed in nginx 1.29.7: upstreams default to HTTP/1.1 with 32 idle keepalive connections per worker; before, each proxied request opened a new HTTP/1.0 connection unless configured. HTTP/2 to upstreams arrived in 1.29.4.
  • What won't change: to choose per request, the proxy must decrypt and parse every request.

On the wire

An illustrative nginx (1.29.7 or later) front for two pods: not run here, but every default in the comments is from the nginx docs (Nov 2026).

upstream orders {
    least_conn;                        # default is round robin, weighted
    server 10.0.1.10:8080;
    server 10.0.1.11:8080;
    # keepalive 32 is the default since 1.29.7: idle upstream connections per worker
}
server {
    listen 443 ssl;                    # TLS ends here: the price of reading paths
    location /api/ {
        proxy_pass http://orders;
        proxy_next_upstream error timeout http_503;  # default is "error timeout"
        proxy_next_upstream_tries 2;   # default 0 means every server in the group
        # non_idempotent is absent: a POST that reached a pod is never resent
    }
}

The defaults that bite are the ones you don't write: unlimited tries, and timeouts counted as retryable.

Measure it

  • See it: nginx $upstream_addr in the access log: a retried request logs two addresses, 10.0.1.11:8080, 10.0.1.10:8080.
  • In production: per target, requests and p99 (per request); ALB HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count against HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count, so you know whether the proxy or the pod produced the error.
  • Bounded by: retry amplification in a partial outage → retry idempotent methods only, cap tries, and use a retry budget (retries done right); a bad pod → outlier ejection.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: An L7 balancer ends TLS, parses each request, matches a route and picks a backend per request from its own connection pool. So one long-lived client connection still spreads across every pod, a failed connect can be retried elsewhere, and errors come back as statuses per route. The catches are in the defaults: ALB downgrades to HTTP/1.1 toward targets, and retries are safe only for requests that never reached a backend or are idempotent.

Q · Mechanism — What changes for the backend when an L7 hop is added? Its peer is now the proxy: a few pooled connections carry many clients' requests, so the client address arrives in X-Forwarded-For. One client's requests arrive on different connections, so state kept per connection breaks. The protocol may change too: an HTTP/2 client behind ALB reaches the pod as HTTP/1.1 unless the target group says otherwise.

Q · Trade-off — ALB or NLB in front of a mesh's ingress gateway? If the gateway (usually Envoy) already routes, retries and terminates TLS, a second L7 tier duplicates that with a second set of timeouts. NLB in front keeps the hop cheap, and the gateway does L7 once. An ALB earns its place when you want managed WAF and OIDC at the edge and the gateway isn't a well-run component yet. Gateway vs LB vs ingress owns the wider comparison.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
ALB idle timeout 60 s settable; long streams need it raised default (as of Nov 2026): AWS ALB attributes
ALB client keepalive 3,600 s maximum client connection lifetime default (as of Nov 2026): AWS ALB attributes
nginx tries to next server unlimited (0) every server in the group can be tried default (as of Nov 2026): nginx docs
Envoy num_retries 1 only once a retry_policy exists default (as of Nov 2026): Envoy route API

Pitfalls

  • "The L7 balancer can retry anything that fails"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it sees every request and response, so hiding a failed pod looks free.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: once a POST reached a backend, the proxy can't know whether it ran, and resending duplicates the side effect; nginx refuses by default.
    ↳ Think instead: retry what never arrived or is idempotent, and carry an idempotency key for the rest.
  • Not the same: a 502 from the balancer vs a 502 from the pod
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: the client sees the same status line either way.
    ↳ Difference: ALB counts the 5xx it generates itself in HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count and the pod's own in HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count.
    ↳ Think instead: split every 5xx graph by origin before deciding which side to debug.
  • "The client speaks HTTP/2, so the pods do too"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the listener shows HTTP/2.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: ALB sends HTTP/1.1 to targets by default (as of Nov 2026), and switching the target group to HTTP/2 makes HTTP/1.1 clients fail.
    ↳ Think instead: the protocol is chosen per hop; check both sides of the balancer.
  • Don't stack a second L7 tier in front of a mesh gateway.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: an ALB in front feels safer.
    ↳ What goes wrong: two retrying hops multiply attempts (three at each is nine), and two idle timeouts disagree.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: an NLB in front, and one L7 tier that owns retries and timeouts.
  • Shelf life: per-request balancing and the retry-safety rule are durable; ALB algorithms, protocol options and proxy defaults move.

Connections

Path:L4 load balancingL7 load balancingthe tradeoff tablealgorithms
  • Builds on L4 vs L7: why a per-request decision needs a parsed request.
  • Owned elsewhere: method properties decide which retries are legal; TLS termination owns the termination models.
  • Used by gRPC and HTTP/2 balancing: an L7 hop is the standard fix for pinning.
  • Breaks when combined with streaming responses: buffering and idle timeouts cut token streams.

notes.title: L4 vs L7 Load Balancing — The Tradeoff Table, the Products and the Decision Tree
notes.html:
References

AWS: How Network Load Balancers work · AWS: ALB target groups · Envoy: TLS Inspector · nginx: ngx_stream_proxy_module · 📜 RFC 9849: TLS Encrypted Client Hello

TL;DR

L4 vs L7 owns the core idea: one decision per connection, or one per request. This note is the full table that follows from it, the products on each side, and the order of checks that settles a choice. For HTTP the default is L7, and every L4 leaf has to name its reason: the traffic isn't HTTP, no intermediary may decrypt, or you need a static IP or the client's address on the socket.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverdesign time
Flow:is it HTTP or gRPC?L4may infrastructure decrypt?L4 pass-through, route by SNIneed a static IP or the socket's client IP?L4 in front of L7otherwise L7

Recall

Prompt Answer
What can a keyless L4 box route on beyond addresses? The SNI hostname in the ClientHello; never the path. ECH hides SNI too.
Static IP for a partner allow-list, and path routing? NLB with its static IPs, an ALB registered as its target.
Which product termination breaks "L4 keeps TLS end to end"? An NLB TLS listener: it decrypts.
ALB → NLB migration: which request header disappears? X-Forwarded-For: no L7 hop adds it.
Two L7 tiers, 3 tries each: attempts on the backend? Up to 9.
Draw by hand: the decision tree HTTP? → may decrypt? → static IP or socket IP? → L7 default.

The idea

Five decisions, each walked through the checks in order. The first check that admits only one answer ends it.

Situation The checks that decide Choice One-sentence defence
A Postgres endpoint for a partner's VPC not HTTP L4 (NLB or a pooler) L7 has no vocabulary for the protocol, so none of its features apply.
Messaging backend; infrastructure must never hold plaintext HTTP, but no intermediary may decrypt L4 pass-through, pools chosen by SNI L7 needs the key; if holding it is disqualifying, the L7 conversation is over.
8 gRPC callers, 40 inference pods HTTP/2, may decrypt, long-lived connections L7 that speaks HTTP/2 upstream 8 connections can occupy at most 8 of 40 pods; only a per-request pick spreads work.
Browser REST API, path routing to 3 services HTTP, may decrypt, path routing needed L7 routing by path isn't expressible below L7.
Partner allow-lists one IP; the API needs path routing HTTP, may decrypt, static IP required NLB in front of ALB each tier does what only it can: the IP at L4, the request at L7.

The trade: L7 sees and decides per request, and you pay with a TLS termination, a parse per request and a plaintext boundary; L4 stays cheap, sealed and protocol-agnostic, and you pay with blindness to everything inside.

How it works

The whole comparison. Every row follows from what the box reads and how often it decides.

Dimension L4 (TCP, UDP) L7 (HTTP) Decides it when
Reads addresses, ports; SNI and ALPN if it peeks method, path, headers, body routing by path or header → L7 only
Decides per flow, fixed at the first packet request many requests per connection → L7
TLS passes through, or a TLS listener terminates terminates, holds the certificate no intermediary may decrypt → L4 pass-through
Client IP at the backend on the socket for pass-through; a proxy needs PROXY protocol in X-Forwarded-For; the socket shows the proxy backend needs it without trusting a header → L4
Health check depth port accepts a connection status and body of a real request "port up, app broken" must be caught → L7 (health checks)
Retries none: no request boundary before the response, idempotent methods failures hidden from clients → L7
Algorithms flow hash, round robin, least connections plus least outstanding requests, EWMA, header hash uneven request cost → L7 (algorithms)
Protocols anything over TCP, UDP, QUIC HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, gRPC; HTTP/3 where supported Postgres, Kafka, MQTT, game traffic → L4
Failure the client sees reset or empty reply 502, 503, 504 clients and dashboards need a status → L7
Logs addresses, bytes, duration method, path, status, upstream, timings triage by route → L7
Addressing (AWS) NLB: a static IP per AZ, Elastic IP if public ALB: a DNS name client configured with an IP → NLB, possibly in front of ALB
Idle timeout (AWS) NLB TCP 350 s, settable 60–6,000 s ALB 60 s long quiet streams: raise the L7 one, or keepalives
Products NLB, nginx stream, HAProxy mode tcp, IPVS, Maglev ALB, Envoy, nginx http, HAProxy mode http Envoy and HAProxy do both, per listener

AWS rows are defaults as of Nov 2026. The decision tree runs the checks in the order that ends them soonest:

  • L4: changes if the protocol grows an HTTP front, such as a REST API beside the database.
  • L4 pass-through: changes if the rule relaxes to "encrypted on every hop", which re-encryption after an L7 hop satisfies (termination models).
  • L4 in front of L7: changes if clients can use a DNS name; then one ALB is less to run.
  • L7: changes only for packet rates where per-request state is the bottleneck, which inside a datacentre is rare for HTTP.

Evolution

Lineage:2016 Maglev, Google's software L4 balancer (NSDI)Aug 2016 AWS ALBSep 2017 AWS NLBMar 2026 RFC 9849, Encrypted Client Hello
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): every cloud sells both tiers, and Envoy, nginx and HAProxy run both modes in one binary.
  • Changed in RFC 9849: with ECH, the real hostname travels encrypted, so an L4 box that routed on SNI sees only the public outer name and must route on that or move to L7.
  • What won't change: to act on a request you have to read it, and reading it means holding the key.

On the wire

One Envoy listener doing both, as an illustrative excerpt (not run here; field names from the Envoy v3 API docs, Nov 2026). The TLS inspector reads the hostname without a key, then each filter chain picks a mode.

listener_filters:
- name: envoy.filters.listener.tls_inspector        # reads SNI and ALPN from the ClientHello, no key
  typed_config:
    "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.listener.tls_inspector.v3.TlsInspector
filter_chains:
- filter_chain_match: {server_names: ["db.example.com"]}
  filters:                                         # L4: choose a cluster by hostname, relay ciphertext
  - name: envoy.filters.network.tcp_proxy
    typed_config:
      "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.network.tcp_proxy.v3.TcpProxy
      stat_prefix: db
      cluster: db_pool
- filter_chain_match: {server_names: ["api.example.com"]}
  transport_socket:                                # L7: terminate TLS; this chain holds the certificate
    name: envoy.transport_sockets.tls
  filters:
  - name: envoy.filters.network.http_connection_manager   # parse requests, then route by path

The same port serves both: the hostname picks the chain, and only the second chain can see a path.

Break it: a forwarder with no key sits between a TLS 1.3 client and backend on 127.0.0.1 and records every byte it relays. The client asks for GET /orders/42 on api.example.test.

def pipe(a, b):
    while (d := a.recv(65536)): relayed.extend(d); b.sendall(d)   # the L4 box: copy, never decrypt
# ... client wraps with server_hostname="api.example.test", sends GET /orders/42
print(b"api.example.test" in relayed, b"/orders" in relayed)
# look for: the hostname is in the relayed bytes, the path isn't
# naive belief predicts: False, False ("L4 sees nothing"), or True, True ("it's all on the wire")

Run twice on Python 3.15 with OpenSSL 4.0.3: 4,094 bytes relayed, hostname visible, path not, while the backend read GET /orders/42. Under TLS 1.3 the certificate is encrypted too, so the name came from the ClientHello's SNI: enough to choose a pool, never a route.

Measure it

  • See it: stop a backend and ask each tier: a status code means L7, curl: (52) or a reset means L4. For SNI routing, openssl s_client -servername with two names should reach two pools.
  • In production: per backend, max over median requests per second; near 1 at L7 with least-request, high behind L4 with few long-lived clients. A flat 5xx floor near 1/n of traffic points to a shallow health check.
  • Bounded by: a pinned connection → per-request balancing or a maximum connection age (gRPC and HTTP/2 balancing); retry storms across tiers → one tier owns retries, with a budget.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: The choice is what the balancer may see. L4 reads addresses, ports and at most the SNI hostname, picks once per flow and keeps TLS sealed. L7 decrypts and picks per request, which buys routing, retries, deep health checks and statuses. For HTTP I default to L7 and make L4 earn its place: non-HTTP traffic, no decryption allowed, or a static IP, in which case NLB goes in front of ALB.

Q · Mechanism — Why can an L4 box route by hostname but not by path? The hostname is in the ClientHello's SNI extension, sent before any key exists so the server can choose a certificate; Envoy's TLS inspector reads it with no key, as the run above shows. The path is inside the encrypted application data. Reading it means terminating TLS and parsing HTTP, and a box that does both is L7 by definition. Encrypted Client Hello (RFC 9849) closes even the hostname to boxes without the ECH key.

Q · Trade-off — Same HTTP service: when does L4 become the wrong answer? Traffic shape, not volume, flips it. Browsers send a few requests per connection over thousands of connections, and a flow hash spreads that acceptably. Services on HTTP/2 or with deep connection pools send thousands of requests per connection, and one decision governs all of them: the flow-count arithmetic leaves a third of a fleet idle when connections equal backends. The second flip is request cost spread: 2 ms and 2 s requests can't be balanced by counting connections.

Q · Failure — You move an internal API from ALB to NLB to save cost. What breaks first? The health check's depth. ALB's GET /healthz returned 503 when the database pool was exhausted; the NLB's TCP check sees an open port and keeps the pod in service. The error rate settles at a flat share near 1/n and stays, with every target healthy. Then X-Forwarded-For disappears, so IP-based limits key on whatever the socket shows, and idle timeouts change from 60 s to 350 s. Confirm with per-target 5xx and health-check type; fix with an HTTP check on the NLB target group.

Q · Design — A SaaS edge: partners allow-list static IPs, tenants bring custom domains, services talk gRPC inside. Place the tiers. The binding constraint is the static IP, so an NLB holds the addresses and forwards to an L7 tier. That tier selects tenant certificates by SNI, terminates, and routes per request; tenants who demand that no one decrypts get an SNI pass-through chain instead. Inside, gRPC rides a mesh or an L7 proxy that speaks HTTP/2 upstream, never a plain L4 Service. Watch per-pod request skew on the gRPC path first: it regresses silently the day someone adds an L4 hop. The service view is in communication patterns.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Pods reachable by 8 connections ≤ 8 of 40 one pick per connection derived
Attempts on a backend, two tiers × 3 tries up to 9 retries multiply across hops derived
NLB TCP idle timeout 350 s (60–6,000 s) then RST on the next packet default (as of Nov 2026): AWS NLB docs
ALB idle timeout 60 s a quiet stream is closed default (as of Nov 2026): AWS ALB attributes
ALB protocol to targets HTTP/1.1 HTTP/2 or gRPC by target group default (as of Nov 2026): AWS ALB target groups
Keyless forwarder, TLS 1.3 hostname visible, path not 4,094 bytes relayed measured: Python 3.15, OpenSSL 4.0.3, 22 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • Not the same: an NLB TLS listener vs TLS pass-through
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "layer 4" products on the same NLB, and the console offers TLS as a listener protocol.
    ↳ Difference: a TLS listener terminates at the balancer, which then holds the certificate; a TCP listener relays the ciphertext and the backend terminates.
    ↳ Think instead: ask which box holds the private key, not which layer the product is named after.
  • "L4 vs L7 is a performance decision"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: "L4 is faster" is the first line of most comparisons.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the parse cost is per request and small next to backend work; what changes is what the balancer can see, so routing, retries, statuses and spread change with it.
    ↳ Think instead: a visibility decision with performance consequences; measure the hop if latency is really in question.
  • "An L4 box can't route by name"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it never decrypts, so it seems to know nothing about the request.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the SNI hostname travels in clear in the ClientHello, and the run above read it from relayed bytes, and Envoy's TLS inspector routes on it without a key.
    ↳ Think instead: hostname yes, path no, and ECH takes the hostname away too.
  • "Moving to L7 evens out the load by itself"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: L7 decides per request, which fixes the pinning that L4 caused.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: round robin per request still sends a 2 s report to a pod already running two, because it counts requests, not work.
    ↳ Think instead: per-request picks plus a load-aware algorithm, least outstanding requests or EWMA.
  • Don't swap an ALB for an NLB just to save money.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the service "only needs TCP", and an L4 hop looks simpler and cheaper.
    ↳ What goes wrong: health checks get shallower, X-Forwarded-For and statuses vanish, and the flat 5xx floor costs more than the balancer did.
    ↳ Do instead: keep the ALB unless one of the tree's L4 reasons applies, and re-home every check it did.
  • Don't run two tiers when one will do.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: NLB in front of ALB is the pattern large platforms draw.
    ↳ What goes wrong: two hops, two idle timeouts and two places to debug, for a static IP nobody asked for.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: one ALB behind a DNS name, until a client really needs a fixed address.
  • Shelf life: the table's logic is durable; AWS defaults, protocol options and product names move, and ECH keeps shrinking what L4 can read.

Connections

Path:L4 load balancingL7 load balancingthe tradeoff tablealgorithms
  • Builds on L4 vs L7: connection or request, and the capture of both boxes.
  • Owned elsewhere: health checks own check depth; TLS termination owns termination models; reverse proxy responsibilities own header rewriting.
  • Bounded by gRPC and HTTP/2 balancing: the fixes for pinned connections.
  • Composes with API gateway and service mesh: where the L7 decision lives once it's chosen.
  • Decided in communication patterns: gateway and mesh placement.

notes.title: Load Balancing Algorithms — Turn Order, In-Flight Requests, Two Choices, Latency
notes.html:
References

Envoy: Supported load balancers · nginx: ngx_http_upstream_module · AWS: Edit target group attributes (routing algorithms, slow start) · Mitzenmacher 2001: The Power of Two Choices in Randomized Load Balancing · Envoy: Peak EWMA

TL;DR

The algorithm picks one healthy backend using what it can see: turn order, open connections, in-flight requests, or latency times in-flight. The more it sees, the less queueing when request cost varies; the price is state that goes stale. Least request over two random picks is the L7 default; hashing answers a different question.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:request arriveshealthy set from the checkersample 2 hostspick fewer in-flightforward, in-flight +1response, in-flight −1a new host ramps up under slow start

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does round robin assume? Every request costs the same and every backend is the same size.
Least connections vs least request? Open sockets vs in-flight requests; HTTP/2 puts many requests on one socket.
Envoy least_request default choice_count? 2: power of two choices, not a full scan.
Peak EWMA's cost function? RTT_peak_ewma × (active_requests + 1), lowest wins.
Who in the middle runs it? The proxy or LB, per request at L7; per connection at L4.
Draw by hand: the signal ladder turn order → open sockets → in-flight → latency × in-flight; P2C samples beside it.

The idea

A search fleet of ten pods runs at 80% load. Nine requests in ten take 10 ms, one takes 300 ms. Round robin hands pod 4 its next request while pod 4 is still on a 300 ms query, so the cheap request waits behind it. In a model of this fleet, round robin's p99 is about 2 s although every pod gets the same request count.

Least request keeps a busy pod out of rotation until it drains. Same fleet, same load: p50 10 ms, p99 about 0.6 s. Nothing got faster: the queue moved out of one pod and into the balancer's choice.

Then the catch. Run ten balancer replicas whose view of in-flight counts lags, and "pick the minimum" sends every arrival to the same host until the view refreshes. Sampling two at random and taking the lighter one survives that lag.

The trade: every step up the ladder buys less queueing for more per-host state, and state that lags turns the cleverest rule into a herd.

How it works

Each algorithm minimises a different signal; the higher rung sees more of the real work.

Two random choices isn't a rung of its own: it is how the higher rungs pick without a full scan, and why they don't herd.

Rule What actually happens
Round robin, weighted A counter mod n; weights give a bigger instance or a canary more turns. Zero state, blind to cost. It is ALB's default routing algorithm (as of Nov 2026).
Least connections Counts sockets, which tracks work only while one connection carries one request. Under HTTP/2 one socket carries many streams; see gRPC load balancing.
Least request Envoy samples choice_count hosts (2) and takes the fewest active requests. With unequal weights it switches to weight ÷ (active + 1)^bias, a host that never fully drains.
Peak EWMA A latency-aware P2C. In Envoy it's a contrib extension that needs its HTTP filter, and a host failing fast looks fast, so it needs outlier detection.
Who in the middle decides The proxy picks per request at L7 and per connection at L4 (L4 vs L7). With stickiness it picks only the first target.

Why a lagging view herds and sampling doesn't, with the model's numbers:

λ = ρ · n / mean cost = 0.8 · 10 / 39 ms ≈ 205 req/s     ← the model's arrival rate
stale window Δ = 300 ms → λ · Δ ≈ 62 arrivals          ← all see the same "least loaded" host
that host clears Δ / mean ≈ 300 / 39 ≈ 8 requests in Δ  ← 62 sent, 8 served: a herd
P2C: P(host in a sample of 2 from 10) = 1 − 36/45 = 0.2 ← it gets at most ≈ 12 of the 62

Evolution

Lineage:1994 balanced allocations (Azar, Broder, Karlin, Upfal)2001 Mitzenmacher's supermarket model2018 nginx random two (1.15.1)2026 nginx open-sources least_time (1.31.0) and sticky (1.29.6)
  • Maturity today: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026). Envoy ships P2C as the default for least request, and ALB offers round robin, least outstanding requests and weighted random.
  • Changed in nginx 1.31.0 (13 May 2026): least_time, the response-time-aware method, left the commercial subscription. slow_start is still commercial-only, and can't be combined with hash, ip_hash or random.
  • What's next and what won't change: backend load reports (Envoy's client-side weighted round robin reads ORCA utilisation) push the signal past latency; a lagging signal stays the core risk.

On the wire

The same intent in Envoy and nginx (illustrative config, not run here; directive names and defaults from the docs as of Nov 2026):

# Envoy cluster: the L7 default
lb_policy: LEAST_REQUEST
least_request_lb_config:
  choice_count: 2              # P2C; the default, shown for the reader
  slow_start_config:
    slow_start_window: 30s     # new or newly healthy hosts ramp up instead of taking a burst

upstream api {
    random two least_conn;     # P2C over connection counts (nginx counts connections, not requests)
    server 10.0.1.11:8080;
    server 10.0.1.12:8080;
}                              # slow_start= needs the commercial build and refuses random

On ALB the default that bites is the opposite: slow start can't be enabled with least outstanding requests or weighted random, so the cost-aware algorithm comes without a warm-up ramp (as of Nov 2026).

Break it: the model behind the numbers above: ten FIFO servers, Poisson arrivals at 80% load, 90% of requests 10 ms and 10% 300 ms, then the same run with the balancer's view refreshed only every 300 ms.

s = rr % n                                       # round robin
s = min(range(n), key=view.__getitem__)          # least request: global minimum (ties random)
a, b = rnd.sample(range(n), 2); s = a if view[a] <= view[b] else b   # P2C
view = live if fresh else view_refreshed_every(0.300)               # what the balancer can see
# look for: least request's p99 with a stale view vs P2C's
# naive belief predicts: scanning all ten always beats sampling two

Run on Python 3.15.0, 200,000 requests, 22 Nov 2026 (a model, not a measurement):

Algorithm Fresh view p50 / p99 View 300 ms stale p50 / p99
Round robin 294 / 1,983 ms same: it reads no view
Random 307 / 2,382 ms same
Least request 10 / 592 ms 293 / 2,338 ms
P2C 79 / 856 ms 226 / 1,116 ms

With fresh counts the full scan wins. With a lagging view it falls to random's tail, while P2C loses far less. That is why Envoy samples.

Measure it

  • See it: per-host active requests in the proxy (Envoy admin /clusters lists rq_active per host); correct is a narrow spread, with no host idle while another queues.
  • In production: per backend, max ÷ median of in-flight requests, beside p99 per request. A rising ratio with flat traffic means a wrong algorithm, a pinned connection or a broken warm-up.
  • Bounded by: a herd on a new or lagging host → P2C plus slow start; a fast-failing host attracting traffic → health checks and outlier detection before any latency-aware rule.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: The algorithm chooses among healthy backends by what it can see. Round robin sees turns and works when every request costs the same. Least connections sees sockets, which HTTP/2 breaks. Least request sees in-flight work, and peak EWMA adds latency. At scale you sample two hosts instead of scanning all, because a full scan over a stale view herds. The default: least request, two choices, slow start.

Q · Mechanism — Why do a dozen balancer replicas running "least loaded" overload one backend? Each replica decides from its own view of in-flight counts, and that view lags real work. Between refreshes they agree on the same minimum and all send there. In the derivation above, 62 arrivals land on a host that can clear 8 in the window. Sampling two at random puts that host in only one sample in five, so the herd breaks up while busy hosts are still avoided. In the model, a 300 ms stale view takes the full scan's p99 from 0.6 s to 2.3 s; P2C's stays near 1.1 s.

Q · Trade-off — When is round robin the right answer? When request cost and backend size are both uniform: static files, fixed-cost transforms, health endpoints. Then every algorithm converges, and round robin has no state, no tuning and nothing to go stale. The tipping point is cost variance. Once requests differ by an order of magnitude (search, reports, model inference), turn order queues cheap work behind expensive work, and least request becomes the floor. Weighted round robin covers unequal instance sizes, not unequal requests.

Q · Failure — After every deploy, p99 spikes for half a minute on the new pods only. What's happening? New pods start with zero in-flight requests, so least request treats them as the best hosts and sends a burst while their caches, connection pools and JIT are cold. What runs out is the new pod's worker slots. Confirm by plotting p99 and in-flight per pod against pod age: the spike tracks age, not traffic. Fix: slow start (Envoy slow_start_window, nginx's commercial slow_start) and readiness that waits for warm-up. On ALB, slow start excludes least outstanding requests, so pick which one you need.

Q · Design — One platform has a stateless API tier, a WebSocket tier and a sharded cache. One algorithm? No: three objectives. The API wants equal queues, so least request with two choices and slow start. The WebSocket tier is pinned per connection anyway, so the choice happens once per connect: least connections fits, and what matters is draining on deploy (WebSocket in operation). The cache wants each key on one node, which is consistent hashing, accepting imbalance. Watch max ÷ median in-flight on the API tier first. The flash-sale design shows where the balancer sits.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Envoy choice_count 2 P2C is the default for least request default (as of Nov 2026): Envoy cluster docs
Envoy active_request_bias 1.0 weight ÷ (active + 1)^bias when weights differ default (as of Nov 2026): Envoy LB docs
Choices beyond two constant factor only d = 2 is an exponential gain over d = 1; d = 3 adds a constant spec: Mitzenmacher 2001
Least request p99, fresh vs 300 ms stale 592 vs 2,338 ms model above measured: model, Python 3.15.0, 22 Nov 2026
P2C p99, same 856 vs 1,116 ms model above measured: model, Python 3.15.0, 22 Nov 2026
Herd size in one stale window ≈ 62 sent, ≈ 8 served λ ≈ 205 req/s, Δ = 300 ms derived

Pitfalls

  • "Round robin is fair"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: every backend gets the same number of requests, and that's what the dashboard counts.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it's fair in turns, not in work; with 10 ms and 300 ms requests mixed, its model p99 is over three times least request's.
    ↳ Think instead: balance the signal that tracks work, in-flight requests at least, whenever request cost varies.
  • Not the same: least connections vs least request
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both pick "the least busy" host, and on HTTP/1.1 they agree.
    ↳ Difference: one counts sockets, the other requests in flight; HTTP/2 puts many requests on one socket, and L4 sees only sockets.
    ↳ Think instead: at L4 you get connections; at L7 ask for requests.
  • "Checking every backend beats sampling two"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: more information should mean a better choice.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the information lags, and every replica sees the same minimum; in the model, a 300 ms lag takes the full scan's p99 to random's level.
    ↳ Think instead: sample two, take the lighter: almost all the gain, none of the herd.
  • Don't turn on a latency-aware algorithm without outlier detection.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: routing away from slow hosts sounds strictly better.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a host returning instant 503s has the lowest latency in the fleet and attracts the most traffic; Envoy's own docs warn about this.
    ↳ Do instead: health checks and outlier detection first, then peak EWMA or least_time.
  • Don't reach past round robin when requests really are uniform.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: least request is "the default", so it feels safer everywhere.
    ↳ What goes wrong: nothing improves, and on ALB you lose slow start, which least outstanding requests can't be combined with.
    ↳ Do instead: keep round robin plus slow start for fixed-cost endpoints; earn the cost-aware algorithm with measured variance.
  • "A new pod with nothing in flight is the best target"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: zero active requests is literally the minimum.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: cold caches and pools make its first requests slow, and least request sends it a burst at that moment.
    ↳ Think instead: an empty host is cold, not idle: ramp it with slow start.
  • Shelf life: the ladder and the herding argument are durable; which products ship which algorithm, and which are commercial-only, move every year.

Connections

Path:L4 vs L7load balancing algorithmsconsistent hashingsticky sessionshealth checks
  • Builds on L7 load balancing: per-request decisions make in-flight counts visible.
  • Owned elsewhere: queueing theory owns why variance builds queues; consistent hashing owns key-stable routing.
  • Composes with health checks: every algorithm here picks only among hosts the checker calls healthy.
  • Bounded by outlier detection: ejects the fast-failing host a latency rule would favour.
  • Contrasts with gRPC load balancing: when the connection, not the request, is what got balanced.
  • Decided in flash-sale design: where the balancer sits in a real topology.

notes.title: Consistent Hashing — Rings, Virtual Nodes, Maglev and Bounded Loads
notes.html:
References

Karger et al. 1997: Consistent Hashing and Random Trees · Envoy: Supported load balancers (ring hash, Maglev) · Mirrokni, Thorup, Zadimoghaddam 2016: Consistent Hashing with Bounded Loads · Eisenbud et al. 2016: Maglev

TL;DR

hash(key) % n sends almost every key somewhere new when n changes. Consistent hashing puts hosts and keys on one ring and gives each key to the next host clockwise, so adding or losing one host moves about 1/n of the keys. It evens out the key space, not the load: virtual nodes fix the spread, bounded loads fix hot keys.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:route names the key (header, cookie, IP)hash to a 64-bit pointnext host point clockwisethat host
a host leavesonly its arcs change ownereach moves to the next point clockwise

Recall

Prompt Answer
Add an 11th node: keys moved by % n vs a ring? ≈ 91% vs ≈ 9% (model below, matches n/(n+1) and 1/(n+1)).
Why virtual nodes? One point per host leaves arcs uneven: max ÷ mean share 3.06 with one, 1.04 with a thousand.
Envoy hash_balance_factor: 150 means? No host takes more than 1.5 × the cluster's average load; overflow probes onward.

The idea

A ten-node cache tier sits behind hash(key) % 10. You add an eleventh node. A key stays put only when h % 10 == h % 11, so about 91% of keys move at once, those reads all miss, and the database takes the full read load in the same minute.
