On a ring the new node takes a few arcs from its neighbours and nothing else moves: about 9% of keys, its fair share.

The trade: you give up even load for a stable key-to-host mapping, so it only pays when the backend holds state built from the key.

How it works

One key's lookup, and what a host removal changes:

Only B's arcs change owner; keys on every other arc keep their host.

Rule What actually happens
Who in the middle hashes The proxy, on a key the route names: a header, cookie or source IP. nginx needs hash $key consistent; without consistent it remaps most keys.
Virtual nodes Envoy places each host on the ring many times, in proportion to its weight. minimum_ring_size defaults to 1,024 entries, the maximum to 8M; watch min_hashes_per_host and max_hashes_per_host.
Maglev A fixed 65,537-entry lookup table instead of a ring: about 10× faster to build and 5× faster to pick than a 256K ring, but about twice as many keys move when hosts change (Envoy's figures).
Bounded loads hash_balance_factor (minimum 100, typically 120–200) caps each host at that percentage of the average. A request for a full host probes onward with a random jump, so a hot key spills instead of melting one node.

Why the gap widens with fleet size:

modulo, n → n+1: a key stays only if h % n = h % (n+1) → moved ≈ n/(n+1)   ← 90.9% at n = 10
ring, n → n+1:  the new host takes its fair share     → moved ≈ 1/(n+1)   ← 9.1% at n = 10
at n = 100:     modulo ≈ 99%, ring ≈ 1%                                   ← bigger fleets suffer more under %

Evolution

Lineage:1997 Karger et al., consistent hashing for web caches2014 jump consistent hash (Lamping, Veach)2016 Maglev (NSDI)2016 bounded loads (Mirrokni, Thorup, Zadimoghaddam)
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): Envoy ships ring hash (xxHash by default) and Maglev, both with bounded loads; nginx ships ketama via hash … consistent.
  • What won't change: every key-stable scheme trades evenness for stability.

On the wire

Envoy cluster config for a cache tier (illustrative; field names and defaults from the Envoy docs, Nov 2026). The route must also carry a hash_policy naming the key:

lb_policy: RING_HASH
ring_hash_lb_config:
  minimum_ring_size: 4096     # default 1,024; more points per host, smoother arcs
common_lb_config:
  consistent_hashing_lb_config:
    hash_balance_factor: 125  # no host above 1.25 × the average; overflow spills onward

A model of the same choices (Python 3.15.0, 22 Nov 2026; 50,000 keys on 10 nodes, then 200,000 Zipf-distributed requests; a model, not a measurement):

add 1 node to 10:      modulo moved 91.0%   ring (160 points/host) 9.2%   jump 9.2%
max ÷ mean key share:  1 point 3.06   10 points 1.41   100 points 1.16   1,000 points 1.04
Zipf requests:         ring max ÷ mean load 1.58   bounded (c = 1.25) 1.25

Popular keys pushed one node to 1.58 × average until the bound capped it.

Measure it

  • See it: keys moved per membership change, sampled offline; correct is about 1/n, more means too few points or an unstable key.
  • In production: per node, hit ratio and requests per second; one node far above the mean is a hot key; a fleet-wide hit-ratio dip on every deploy is remapping.
  • Bounded by: a hot key melting one node → hash_balance_factor, or splitting the key; a flapping host thrashing the ring → health checks with hysteresis.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Modulo hashing remaps almost every key when the node count changes, which empties a cache tier at once. Consistent hashing puts nodes and keys on a ring, so a change moves only about 1/n of the keys. Virtual nodes even out the arcs; bounded loads cap hot keys. It gives up load equalisation, so use it only when the backend keeps state derived from the key.

Q · Mechanism — What exactly moves when a node dies? Only the keys in that node's arcs, each to the next point clockwise. With one point per node, the whole share lands on one successor, which can double its load. With many virtual points the arcs are scattered, so the keys spread across most survivors. The traffic that moves follows popularity, not key count (pitfall below).

Q · Trade-off — Consistent hashing or least request in front of a cache? Least request equalises CPU but scatters each key across nodes, so every node caches the same hot keys and useful memory shrinks toward one node's worth. Hashing keeps each key on one node, so useful memory is the sum of the nodes, at the cost of hot spots and remapping on every change. The tipping point is state built from the key: caches, shards, rate-limit counters hash; stateless work uses least request.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Envoy minimum_ring_size / maximum 1,024 / 8M entries ring hash default (as of Nov 2026): Envoy cluster docs
Envoy Maglev table size 65,537 fixed; ≈ 2 × the movement of ring hash default (as of Nov 2026): Envoy LB docs
hash_balance_factor ≥ 100, typically 120–200 unbounded if unset default (as of Nov 2026): Envoy cluster docs

Pitfalls

  • "Consistent hashing spreads load evenly"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: with enough virtual nodes every host owns an equal arc.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: equal key space isn't equal traffic; in the Zipf model one node carried 1.58 × the average.
    ↳ Think instead: even keys, uneven load: add a load bound when popularity is skewed.
  • Not the same: 1/n of keys vs 1/n of traffic
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: the guarantee is quoted as "only 1/n is affected".
    ↳ Difference: the guarantee counts keys; traffic follows popularity, so losing the node with the hot keys moves far more than 1/n of requests.
    ↳ Think instead: size the successors for the hottest node's traffic, not for its key count.
  • Don't hash in front of stateless backends.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it sounds more sophisticated than least request.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you lose load equalisation and gain hot spots, for stability nothing uses.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: least request with two choices; hash only for state built from the key.
  • Don't hash on a key with few values.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a tenant or region header is already on every request.
    ↳ What goes wrong: three distinct values reach at most three nodes, however many you run.
    ↳ Do instead: hash a high-cardinality key (user, object, session), and check its distribution first.
  • Shelf life: the ring and its 1/n property are durable; Envoy's defaults and its Maglev-vs-ring figures move with releases.

Connections

Path:load balancing algorithmsconsistent hashingsticky sessions
  • Contrasts with load balancing algorithms: they minimise imbalance; hashing minimises remapping.
  • Used by sticky sessions: hashing a session key is affinity without a cookie.
  • Breaks when combined with flapping health checks: every flap is a membership change.
  • Decided in URL shortener: hashing keys across cache and storage nodes.
  • Drilled in shard keys for multi-tenant data: the same idea applied to data placement.

notes.title: Sticky Sessions — Cookie and IP Affinity, and Why It's a Scaling Smell
notes.html:
References

AWS: Edit target group attributes (sticky sessions) · nginx: ngx_http_upstream_module (sticky, ip_hash) · Socket.IO: Using multiple nodes

TL;DR

Affinity pins a client to one backend so state in that backend's memory stays reachable. The balancer reads a cookie it issued, or hashes the client's IP, and skips the algorithm. Every pinned request bypasses balancing, so deploys, scale-in and crashes become user-visible; moving the state out of the pod removes the need.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:first requestalgorithm picks ASet-Cookie: lb=Alater requests skip the algorithmA goes awayalgorithm picks B, cookie rewrittenB has no session: 302 /login

Recall

Prompt Answer
ALB cookie names an unhealthy target: what happens? It picks a new target, rewrites the cookie, and stays there after the old one returns.
nginx ip_hash key for IPv4? The first three octets: a whole /24 lands on one server.
Does a WebSocket need stickiness turned on? No: one connection, already pinned to the target that returned 101.

The idea

A shop keeps carts in pod memory and turns on stickiness so each user returns to the pod holding their cart. Then a rolling deploy replaces pods one by one, each drops every cart it held, and support hears "it logged me out mid-checkout".

With the cart in Redis or a signed token, any pod serves any request and the deploy is invisible.

The trade: affinity makes in-pod state work without a redesign, and you pay with balancing you can't do, deploys users can see and skew you can't fix.

How it works

The exchange as captured from our local balancer (below): the pin holds until its pod goes away.

The balancer re-pinned in one request; the user's state couldn't follow.

Rule What actually happens
Balancer cookie ALB issues AWSALB (1 s to 7 days) and skips the routing algorithm while it's valid. Only the balancer layer that set it can read it.
Application cookie ALB follows your own cookie and issues AWSALBAPP-0…3; it works across balancer layers but not with weighted target groups (as of Nov 2026).
Source-IP hash Works at L4 with no client cooperation. Office egress and carrier NAT put thousands of users on one address, and a phone changing networks breaks the pin.
Hash on a key A session or user header through consistent hashing: a node loss moves only its share.
Who in the middle acts The balancer that issued the pin; every request carrying it skips the algorithm, so the first pick is the only balancing that happens.

What a deploy costs when state lives in the pod:

n pods, S active sessions, each pod holds ≈ S/n      ← the first pick spreads them
lose one pod → ≈ S/n sessions lose state             ← a crash or a scale-in step
roll all n pods within one session lifetime → ≈ S    ← every session's pod is replaced once
state in Redis or a signed token → 0                 ← the pin only reconnects, nothing is lost

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): every major L7 balancer offers cookie affinity.
  • Changed in nginx 1.29.6 (10 Mar 2026): sticky left the commercial subscription, so open-source nginx no longer needs ip_hash for affinity.
  • What won't change: a pin overrides the algorithm, whichever product issues it.

On the wire

Our code on 127.0.0.1: a small Python balancer that pins with an lb cookie, in front of two backends holding sessions in memory. curl -i with a cookie jar, Python 3.15.0, curl 8.7.1, 22 Nov 2026:

GET /login                          → 200 OK
Set-Cookie: sid=d30cc72f            ← the app's session, held in pod A's memory
Set-Cookie: lb=A                    ← the balancer's pin
GET /cart  (Cookie: sid, lb=A)      → 200 OK  "cart on A"   ← algorithm skipped
# pod A stopped
GET /cart  (Cookie: sid, lb=A)      → 302 Found
Location: /login                    ← pod B has never seen sid=d30cc72f
Set-Cookie: lb=B                    ← re-pinned in one request, session lost anyway

The balancer behaved as ALB's docs describe; the failure is where the state lived.

Measure it

  • See it: curl -i with a cookie jar; correct is one balancer cookie on the first response and the same backend after, as in the capture.
  • In production: per backend, requests and sessions; max ÷ mean far above 1 means pins outlived their load. Logins spiking per deploy mean state in the pod.
  • Bounded by: lost state on pod loss → externalise the session; skew from old pins → a short stickiness duration; NAT skew → a cookie or key hash instead of ip_hash.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Affinity sends a client back to the same backend, by a balancer cookie or a hash of something stable like the IP. While the pin holds, the balancer skips its algorithm. It works, but it turns a stateless tier stateful: deploys and scale-in drop sessions, and load stays where the first pick put it. Move the state to Redis or a signed token, and keep affinity only where the protocol needs it.

Q · Mechanism — Cookie affinity or IP hash: what really differs? A cookie names one client and one target, with an expiry the balancer sets; it needs L7, and a client that drops cookies gets a new pick each time. IP hash needs nothing from the client and works at L4, but it's coarse both ways: nginx hashes an IPv4 client's whole /24, so an office or a carrier NAT pool lands on one server, while a phone moving from Wi-Fi to cellular loses its pin.

Q · Trade-off — A WebSocket chat tier: does it need sticky sessions? The socket doesn't: it's one connection, pinned to whichever target answered 101, and what it needs is a long idle timeout and draining (WebSocket in operation). Stickiness is needed when one logical session spans several requests, such as Socket.IO's long-polling fallback. The design question is the room: two users on different pods must still see each other's messages, so add a pub/sub fan-out layer rather than hoping they share a pod.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
ALB stickiness duration 1 s – 7 days both cookie types default (as of Nov 2026): AWS ALB docs
AWSALB cookie's own expiry 7 days, not configurable separate from the duration default (as of Nov 2026): AWS ALB docs
nginx ip_hash key first 3 octets of IPv4, all of IPv6 a /24 shares a server spec: nginx docs

Pitfalls

  • "WebSocket needs sticky sessions enabled on the balancer"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: WebSocket guides mention stickiness, and the socket is stateful.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the connection is already pinned to the target that returned 101; what needs stickiness is a session spanning several HTTP requests, like a long-polling fallback.
    ↳ Think instead: sockets pin themselves; turn stickiness on only for multi-request transports.
  • Not the same: the balancer's cookie vs the app's session cookie
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are cookies set on the first response, and both mention "session".
    ↳ Difference: AWSALB or lb=A names a target; sid names state. Re-pinning is instant, but the state stays on the old pod.
    ↳ Think instead: the pin routes, it doesn't carry state; losing the pod loses the session.
  • Don't use ip_hash for public traffic.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it needs no cookies and works for any client.
    ↳ What goes wrong: nginx keys on the /24, so a large office or carrier NAT pool puts thousands of users on one backend, skew you can't see in your own logs.
    ↳ Do instead: a balancer cookie, or a hash of a user or session key.
  • Don't use affinity to hide in-memory state.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's a checkbox, and the redesign is a sprint.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every deploy and scale-in logs users out, and load can't be rebalanced.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler, durable fix: session in Redis or a signed token, then turn stickiness off.
  • Shelf life: the bypass and its costs are durable; cookie names, duration limits and which nginx build has sticky change.

Connections

Path:consistent hashingsticky sessionshealth checks
  • Builds on load balancing algorithms: a pin bypasses whichever one you chose.
  • Contrasts with consistent hashing: deliberate key placement instead of a workaround for in-pod state.
  • Composes with draining and graceful shutdown: what makes losing a pinned pod survivable.
  • Owned elsewhere: WebSocket owns why one socket is one backend.
  • Drilled in how an MCP client connects: dropping sessions removed the need for sticky routing.

notes.title: Health Checks — Active vs Passive, Shallow vs Deep, and Failing Open
notes.html:
References

Amazon Builders' Library: Implementing health checks · Envoy: Health checking · Envoy: Panic threshold · AWS: ALB target group health checks

TL;DR

A health check decides which backends the balancing algorithm may pick from, so it is a control loop that changes routing, not a dashboard. Check what is local to the instance, never a dependency every instance shares, or one database blip ejects the whole fleet at once. When most backends look unhealthy, the checker is the likelier liar: fail open.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:probe every intervalcount consecutive resultsunhealthy_threshold failuresout of the candidate sethealthy_threshold passesback in
healthy share falls below the panic thresholdbalancer ignores healthroutes to every host

Recall

Prompt Answer
Active vs passive? Active probes on a timer; passive judges real responses (outlier detection).
Detection time, ALB defaults? 30–65 s: two failed probes 30 s apart, plus the 5 s timeout.
Envoy's panic threshold? 50% by default: below it, health status is ignored.
When does an ALB fail open? Only when every target in every enabled AZ is unhealthy.
Who in the middle acts on this? The balancer: it removes the target from the set every request picks from.
Draw by hand: the correlated ejection LB probes three pods; each deep check touches one DB; DB blips; all three ejected.

The idea

Six pods serve an orders API behind a balancer. Someone makes /health "honest" by adding a database ping. One Tuesday the database stalls for a second: every pod fails the same check at the same moment, the balancer ejects all six, and the API returns 503 for everything, though most requests would have succeeded from cache or after one retry. In the run below, that took two probe intervals.

With a local check (thread pool up, config loaded, warm-up done) the same stall shows up as slow requests and a few errors. Every pod stays in rotation, and outlier detection handles the pod that is really broken.

The trade: a deeper check catches more ways one instance can fail, and you pay with correlation; once a check touches anything shared, its failures arrive together, which is the one case a balancer cannot route around.

How it works

The balancer probes each pod; the dashed edge is the one that makes a check deep and dangerous.

Every pod that probes the database becomes one failure, not three.

Rule What actually happens
Depth TCP connect proves a listener; a static 200 proves the request path; a local check proves this instance can serve. Shared dependencies stay out (Builders' Library).
Thresholds Consecutive counts, asymmetric on purpose: the ALB ejects after 2 failures and restores after 5 passes, so a flapping target stays out.
Non-matching status in Envoy A status outside expected_statuses marks the host unhealthy at once, ignoring the threshold. Report degradation with x-envoy-degraded, not a 503.
Failing open Envoy ignores health when the healthy share drops below 50%. An ALB or NLB does so only when every target is unhealthy.
Who in the middle acts on it The balancer. An ejected target gets no new requests; NLB also drops an AZ's IP from DNS when that AZ has no healthy target.

The arithmetic to do before an incident, with ALB defaults as inputs:

detect = (T − 1)·I … T·I, + timeout        ← failure starts just before or just after a probe
       = 30 … 60 s + 5 s = 30–65 s         ← I = 30 s, unhealthy T = 2, timeout 5 s
restore = (H − 1)·I … H·I = 120–150 s      ← healthy H = 5: slow back in, by design
errors while detecting ≈ 1/n of traffic    ← one dead target of n, round robin
probe load = targets × checkers ÷ I        ← 500 sidecars × 500 endpoints ÷ 5 s = 50,000/s

The last line is why a mesh leans on passive detection rather than having every sidecar probe every endpoint.

Evolution

Lineage:2019 Builders' Library codifies local vs dependency checks and failing open2023 Kubernetes 1.27 makes gRPC probes stable
  • Maturity today: 🟢 Established, Nov 2026. Every balancer and orchestrator probes; Envoy, ALB, NLB, Route 53 and Global Accelerator all fail open in some form.
  • What's next and what won't change: gray failures (slow, partly wrong) push toward passive signals and success-rate ejection. The rule that a shared dependency must not decide membership doesn't change.

On the wire

An annotated Envoy cluster (syntax as in the Envoy 1.41-dev docs, Nov 2026): a local active check with jitter, and the panic threshold written out.

clusters:
- name: orders
  health_checks:
  - timeout: 1s
    interval: 10s
    interval_jitter_percent: 10      # decorrelate probes from many Envoys
    unhealthy_threshold: 2           # required: Envoy has no default
    healthy_threshold: 3             # required; at startup one pass is enough
    no_traffic_interval: 60s         # slower probing for a cluster with no traffic yet
    http_health_check:
      path: /health/local            # this process only: pool, config, warm-up
  common_lb_config:
    healthy_panic_threshold:
      value: 50.0                    # the default, explicit: below 50% healthy, ignore health

Break it: six local backends share one "database" flag; an active checker (interval 0.1 s, unhealthy 2, healthy 3) probes /health/deep or /health/local while the flag is down from 0.5 s to 1.5 s.

def do_GET(self):
    if self.path == "/health/deep": code = 200 if DB_OK["v"] else 503   # touches the shared DB
    else:                           code = 200                          # /health/local
routable = n if n / len(ports) >= panic else len(ports)                 # panic: use all hosts
# look for: deep check → 0 of 6 healthy at once; local check → 6 of 6 throughout
# naive belief predicts: a deeper check removes only the instances that are broken

Run on 22 Nov 2026, Python 3.15.0: the deep check took the fleet to 0 healthy at 0.6 s and back to 6 at 1.8 s, which is the outage end plus three passing probes. With no panic threshold, 0 hosts were routable; with 50%, all 6 stayed routable. The local check never ejected anyone.

Measure it

  • See it: Envoy's /clusters admin endpoint shows health_flags per host; on AWS, describe-target-health gives each target's state and reason. Correct is one host flagged at a time, not a whole group.
  • In production: per target group, healthy-host count as a share of fleet, alerting on a drop within one interval; 503s with no backend log line mean an empty candidate set.
  • Bounded by: a fleet-wide ejection → local-only checks, a panic threshold or fail-open, and jittered probes; a flapping target → asymmetric thresholds that restore slowly.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A health check picks the candidate set every request is balanced across, so it's a control, not monitoring. Active checks probe on a timer; passive ones judge real traffic. Keep active checks local, because a shared dependency in the check makes every instance fail together. Do the arithmetic: ALB defaults take 30–65 s to eject. And fail open: below half healthy, Envoy ignores health.

Q · Mechanism — What does the balancer do when a target fails its check? It counts consecutive failures; at unhealthy_threshold it removes the target from the set the algorithm draws from, so new requests skip it while in-flight ones finish. It keeps probing, often at an unhealthy_interval, and re-admits after healthy_threshold passes. Envoy short-cuts both ways: a status outside expected_statuses ejects at once, and at startup one pass admits. Below the panic threshold it stops trusting the flags altogether.

Q · Trade-off — How aggressive should the thresholds be? Faster ejection means a shorter interval or a threshold of 2, which ejects healthy hosts on a GC pause or a slow disk flush. If several go at once, the survivors take their load and fail the same check. Slow ejection leaves 1/n of traffic failing for the whole detection window. The usual answer is asymmetric: quick out, slow back. Then put outlier detection on top, which reacts within a few real requests, and stop tuning the timer.

Q · Failure — The healthy-host count drops to zero with no deploy, and every request gets 503. What happened? The candidate set ran out: every target failed the same check together, which means something shared, almost always a dependency inside the check. Confirm with per-target reasons in describe-target-health or Envoy's health_flags: identical reasons at the same timestamp, and no application log lines for the 503s because nothing was forwarded. Fix: make the check local, set a panic threshold, add probe jitter. Watch the recovery: the whole fleet comes back cold at once, which is the thundering herd.

Q · Design — Health checking for a GPU inference fleet whose pods take three minutes to load weights. The binding constraint is warm-up: a loading pod must get no traffic and must not be killed. Kubernetes gates traffic with readiness and restarts with liveness; probes vs LB checks owns that split. At the balancer, check local state only: weights loaded and one warm-up inference done, never the model registry. A throttling GPU passes an HTTP check while timing out real calls, so passive ejection on real latency does most of the work. Watch healthy share against fleet size first. The serving design is in resilience patterns.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
ALB interval · timeout 30 s · 5 s instance and IP targets; Lambda differs default (as of Nov 2026): AWS ALB docs
ALB unhealthy · healthy thresholds 2 · 5 NLB uses the same default (as of Nov 2026): AWS ALB, NLB docs
Envoy panic threshold 50% 0% disables panic mode default (as of Nov 2026): Envoy docs
Detection with ALB defaults 30–65 s (T−1)·I … T·I plus timeout derived
Restore with ALB defaults 120–150 s 5 passes at 30 s derived
Shared-dependency stall 6 → 0 healthy in 2 intervals interval 0.1 s, threshold 2 measured: model, Python 3.15.0, 22 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • "A deeper health check is a better health check"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a check that tests the database sounds more truthful than one that returns 200.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: depth adds correlation. A shared dependency fails every instance at once: six of six ejected in two intervals in the run above.
    ↳ Think instead: deep up to the instance boundary; shared dependencies belong in alerts and outlier detection, not in membership.
  • Not the same: Envoy's panic threshold vs an ALB's fail-open
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both "ignore health when everything looks bad".
    ↳ Difference: Envoy routes to all hosts once fewer than 50% are healthy. An ALB fails open only when every target in every enabled AZ is unhealthy, so at 90% unhealthy the last 10% take everything.
    ↳ Think instead: know where your balancer's cliff is, and size the survivors for it.
  • "Fail-open makes deep checks safe"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: if everything fails together, fail-open catches it.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a dependency that is slow or erring at a low rate fails checks now and then, so servers flap in and out without ever all failing, and fail-open never triggers (Builders' Library).
    ↳ Think instead: fail-open is a last resort for total failure; partial dependency trouble still needs local-only checks.
  • Don't return 503 from the health endpoint to mean "degraded" behind Envoy.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: 503 reads as "under strain, send less".
    ↳ What goes wrong: a status outside expected_statuses makes Envoy mark the host unhealthy immediately, skipping the threshold, so one slow moment ejects it.
    ↳ Do instead: return 200 with x-envoy-degraded, or shed load in the request path.
  • Don't build an elaborate deep check to catch "up but wrong".
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it seems to be the only way to see a pod that answers but answers badly.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every extra probe is another way to correlate failures, and synthetic requests miss what real ones hit.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler pair: a local active check for "dead", passive outlier detection on real traffic for "wrong".
  • Shelf life: the depth and correlation argument is durable; vendor defaults, fail-open rules and probe types change, so re-check them every three months.

Connections

Path:balancing algorithmshealth checksoutlier detection and drainingglobal load balancing
  • Builds on balancing algorithms: health decides the set they choose from.
  • Owned elsewhere: probes vs LB checks owns liveness, readiness and startup; cascading failures owns the recovery herd.
  • Composes with outlier detection: passive ejection catches what a synthetic probe can't.
  • Bounded by outlier detection's ejection cap: the companion guard against emptying a pool.
  • Used by global load balancing: the same checks decide which region answers.
  • Decided in resilience patterns: where membership and failover are chosen for a service.

notes.title: Outlier Detection, Proxy Circuit Breaking and Draining
notes.html:
References

Envoy: Outlier detection · Envoy: OutlierDetection proto · Envoy: Circuit breaking · AWS: ALB target groups

TL;DR

Three proxy controls handle a backend that is failing, overloaded or leaving. Outlier detection ejects one bad host after it fails real requests. Envoy's circuit breaker caps outstanding work for the whole cluster and rejects the excess at once. Draining stops new work to a leaving target while in-flight requests finish.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:requestcluster limits: pending, active, retrieslocal 503 + x-envoy-overloaded
under limitspick a host not ejected5 consecutive 5xxeject for 30 s × ejections, at most 10% of hosts

Recall

Prompt Answer
Outlier detection vs circuit breaking? One bad host leaves the pool vs the whole cluster's outstanding work is capped.
Envoy's max_ejection_percent default? 10%, so a fleet can't be ejected by one poison request.
ALB deregistration delay default? 300 s, range 0–3,600 s (as of Nov 2026).

The idea

A reporting client sends a malformed export request and retries it 60 times. Every backend returns 500 for it, because the bug is in the request. Behind a proxy that ejects a host after five consecutive 5xx with no cap, the retries walk the fleet: in the run below, ten of ten hosts were gone after 50 requests, and the healthy traffic had nowhere to go.

Envoy's defaults stop that: at most 10% of a cluster may be ejected, and below the panic threshold health is ignored.

The trade: passive ejection reacts within a few requests instead of a probe window, and you pay by trusting responses that may be the client's fault, so the cap matters as much as the trigger.

How it works

Where each control acts on one request; yellow is the proxy deciding.

Admission is per cluster, before a host is chosen; ejection is per host, after it answers.

Rule What actually happens
What counts as a failure consecutive_5xx counts every 5xx, client-caused ones included. consecutive_gateway_failure counts only 502, 503, 504, but its enforcement defaults to 0%, so it only ejects if you raise it.
How long a host stays out 30 s × times ejected, capped at 300 s, so a repeat offender stays out longer.
Envoy's circuit breaker Per-cluster caps on connections, pending requests and active requests (1,024 each) and parallel retries (3). Past one, the request fails at once. There is no open, half-open or closed state.
Draining A deregistered ALB target gets no new requests while in-flight ones run up to the delay; the pod's side, a preStop sleep, is rollouts and connections.

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): ejection, concurrency caps and deregistration delay are standard in Envoy, its meshes and managed balancers.
  • What won't change: routing (eject one host) and admission (cap the cluster) are separate decisions that need separate controls.

On the wire

The two guards written out, with the defaults that matter (Envoy 1.41-dev docs, Nov 2026):

outlier_detection:
  consecutive_5xx: 5                       # default; counts client-caused 5xx too
  consecutive_gateway_failure: 5           # default count...
  enforcing_consecutive_gateway_failure: 100   # ...but enforcement defaults to 0%
  base_ejection_time: 30s                  # × times ejected, capped by max_ejection_time (300 s)
  max_ejection_percent: 10                 # default; the cap that saves the fleet
circuit_breakers:
  thresholds:
  - max_pending_requests: 1024             # default; set to what the backend can queue
    max_retries: 3                         # default: parallel retries across the cluster

Break it: a model of the consecutive-5xx rule, run against ten local HTTP servers that all return 500 for one request path; one client sends it 60 times, round robin.

code = 500 if self.path == "/report?bad=1" else 200     # the bug is in the request
bad = st in (502, 503, 504) if count_gateway_only else st >= 500
if fails[p] >= 5 and len(ejected) + 1 <= max(1, len(ports) * cap // 100):
    ejected.add(p)
# look for: no cap → every host ejected; 10% cap → one; gateway-only counting → none
# naive belief predicts: ejection removes only hosts that are broken

Run on 22 Nov 2026, Python 3.15.0: with no cap, all 10 hosts were ejected and the pool was empty after 50 requests; with the default 10% cap, 1; counting only gateway failures, 0.

Measure it

  • See it: Envoy's /stats for a cluster: outlier_detection.ejections_active per cluster and upstream_rq_pending_overflow or upstream_rq_active_overflow per request rejected. Correct is a single ejection at a time.
  • In production: per cluster, ejections per minute by type and overflow against request rate; per deploy, resets while draining.
  • Bounded by: a poison request emptying the pool → max_ejection_percent plus the panic threshold; a slow dependency eating every worker → circuit-breaker caps; dropped requests on deploy → a deregistration delay longer than the longest request.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Three proxy controls. Outlier detection ejects one host after consecutive failures on real traffic, for 30 s times its ejection count, and never more than 10% of the cluster by default. Envoy's circuit breaker is concurrency caps that reject excess at once. Draining stops new requests to a leaving target and lets in-flight ones finish, 300 s by default on an ALB.

Q · Mechanism — Envoy calls it circuit breaking, but where's the open and half-open state? There isn't one. Envoy's breakers are caps enforced at the connection pool: connections, pending requests, active requests and parallel retries per cluster. Past a cap, the router fails the request locally and sets x-envoy-overloaded; the breaker "closes" the moment outstanding work drops. The state machine you know, which opens on an error rate, rejects for a cooldown and sends a trial request, belongs to client libraries and is owned by circuit breakers and bulkheads. Outlier detection with growing ejection times behaves like its half-open step, per host.

Q · Trade-off — Count every 5xx, or only gateway failures? consecutive_5xx reacts to anything, client-caused errors included, so it leans on the ejection cap. Gateway failures (502, 503, 504) almost always mean the host or the path to it: the cleaner signal, but you must raise its enforcement from 0%. Pick it when your service returns legitimate 500s for bad input; keep the cap low either way.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Consecutive 5xx · gateway failures 5 · 5 gateway enforcement 0% by default default (as of Nov 2026): Envoy proto docs
Base · max ejection time 30 s · 300 s base × times ejected default (as of Nov 2026): Envoy proto docs
max_ejection_percent 10% at least one host if always_eject_one_host default (as of Nov 2026): Envoy proto docs
Circuit-breaker caps 1,024 conn · pending · active, 3 retries per cluster, per priority default (as of Nov 2026): Envoy proto docs

Pitfalls

  • Not the same: outlier detection vs circuit breaking
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both stop traffic to something struggling.
    ↳ Difference: outlier detection is routing, removing one host while the rest serve. Circuit breaking is admission, capping work sent to all hosts.
    ↳ Think instead: a broken host needs ejection; an overloaded cluster needs a cap.
  • "Gateway-failure ejection is on by default"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: consecutive_gateway_failure has a default of 5 in the docs.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: enforcing_consecutive_gateway_failure defaults to 0%, so Envoy detects the outlier and ejects nothing.
    ↳ Think instead: every outlier rule has a trigger and an enforcement percentage; check both.
  • Don't leave circuit-breaker caps at 1,024 for a backend that handles 50 concurrent requests.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: defaults feel safe.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a cap never reached protects nothing: requests queue until they time out.
    ↳ Do instead: size max_pending_requests and max_requests from what the backend actually sustains, and alert on overflow.
  • Don't reach for a mesh-wide breaker policy when a client timeout would do.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a proxy breaker looks like the proper fix for a slow dependency.
    ↳ What goes wrong: more thresholds to tune, while the caller still waits unbounded.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler control first, a bounded timeout in the caller, then a cap where the backend's limit is known.
  • Shelf life: the routing-versus-admission split is durable; Envoy's fields and defaults change.

Connections

Path:health checksoutlier detection, circuit breaking, drainingglobal load balancing
  • Builds on health checks: the active half, and the panic threshold this cap pairs with.
  • Owned elsewhere: circuit breakers and bulkheads owns the state machine; rollouts owns pod shutdown.
  • Composes with service mesh: where these are set per service as policy.
  • Bounded by timeouts, retries, backoff: retries that feed the retry cap.

notes.title: The gRPC and HTTP/2 Load-Balancing Problem — One Connection, One Backend
notes.html:
References

grpc.io: gRPC Load Balancing · gRPC: Load-balancing policies (pick_first, round_robin) · Kubernetes: Virtual IPs and Service proxies · Kubernetes: Headless Services · Envoy: Supported load balancers

TL;DR

An L4 balancer decides once per connection, and HTTP/2 puts every call on one long-lived connection, so one decision covers thousands of calls and one backend takes them all. The fix is to move the decision to where calls are visible: an L7 proxy or sidecar, or the client itself with every backend address and a balancing policy. Getting the addresses isn't enough: gRPC's default policy sends everything to the first one.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:client dials the Servicekube-proxy picks a pod at random, onceconntrack pins the connectionevery stream goes to that pod
headless ServiceDNS returns every pod IPround_robin opens a subchannel per podeach RPC goes to the next ready one

Recall

Prompt Answer
When does kube-proxy choose a pod? Once, on the new connection; conntrack sends the rest after it.
gRPC's default LB policy? pick_first: every RPC to the first reachable address.
What does clusterIP: None change? No virtual IP; DNS returns one A or AAAA record per ready pod.
When does a gRPC client learn about new pods? On re-resolution, requested when connections fail or close; no timer.
Who in the middle can fix it? Anything that sees HTTP/2 streams: an L7 proxy, a sidecar, the client.
Draw by hand: the pinning sequence Client SYN → kube-proxy picks pod A → all streams to A; pod B idle; alt: one subchannel per pod.

The idea

Five gateway pods call an inference service of forty pods through a Kubernetes Service. Each gateway opens one gRPC channel, so five TCP connections exist, and kube-proxy picked a pod for each when it was opened. Thirty-five pods receive nothing. Every health check passes, error rate is zero, and scaling to sixty pods adds twenty more idle ones. The balancer is doing exactly what its docs say: choosing per connection. HTTP/2 is doing what its RFC says: carrying many streams on one connection.

The mechanism changes when the decision moves to where calls are visible. A headless Service hands the client every pod's address; a round_robin policy keeps a connection to each and sends each call to the next one. Or an L7 proxy terminates the client's HTTP/2 connection, holds its own to every pod, and places each stream.

The trade: per-call balancing costs either a proxy hop on every call or connections from every client to every backend, plus client configuration; without it, adding capacity stops working and nothing reports an error.

How it works

One decision at the SYN covers every later stream; the alt branch is the client-side fix.

The connection count, not the request count, is what an L4 hop distributes.

Rule What actually happens
kube-proxy iptables or nftables rules pick a backend pod at random for each new connection; conntrack keeps the rest of that connection on it.
Headless Service clusterIP: None: no virtual IP and no kube-proxy in the path; DNS returns an A or AAAA record per ready pod.
LB policy pick_first (the default) tries addresses in order and sends every RPC to the first that connects. round_robin holds a subchannel per address and rotates RPCs across the ready ones.
Re-resolution Requested when connections fail or close (gRFC A61), and C-core waits at least 30 s between DNS lookups. New pods appear only after a connection event.
The middle An L7 proxy or sidecar (Envoy, a mesh) ends the client's HTTP/2 connection and places each stream on its own connections to every pod.

Why a better hash doesn't help, and what the client-side fix costs:

L4 decisions = connections c, not calls r        ← kube-proxy picks once per connection
c = 5 gateway channels, n = 40 pods              ← the shape in the idea
busy pods ≤ 5 → idle ≥ 35/40 = 87.5%             ← true for any hash or random pick
expected busy = 40 · (1 − (39/40)^5) ≈ 4.75      ← collisions are ordinary
client-side: m · n = 5 · 40 = 200 connections    ← the cost moves to connection count

Evolution

Lineage:2015 HTTP/2 (RFC 7540)2015 gRPC2017 grpc.io names proxy, client-side and lookaside balancing2020 proxyless xDS (gRFC A27)2024 GRPCRoute GA in Gateway API v1.1
  • Maturity today: 🟢 Established, Nov 2026. The problem and its three families of fix haven't changed since 2017. Linkerd and Istio's sidecars balance HTTP/2 per request; Istio's ambient L4 layer balances per connection only, so gRPC needs a waypoint.
  • Changed with xDS: grpclb, gRPC's original lookaside protocol, is deprecated in favour of xDS, so a control plane now pushes endpoints and policy straight into proxyless clients.
  • What's next and what won't change: inference routers balance on queue depth and cache state. A long-lived multiplexed connection still needs a per-call decision somewhere.

On the wire

Illustrative Kubernetes config: the default that bites is the ClusterIP, and the second is the client's default policy.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: inference-headless }
spec:
  clusterIP: None              # no VIP: DNS answers with every ready pod's IP
  selector: { app: inference }
  ports: [{ port: 50051 }]
# client side, the gRPC service config; without it the channel uses pick_first:
#   target  dns:///inference-headless.default.svc.cluster.local:50051
#   config  {"loadBalancingConfig": [{"round_robin": {}}]}

Break it: three gRPC servers on 127.0.0.1, one channel given all three addresses (what a headless Service's DNS answer holds), 60 calls per policy.

target = "ipv4:127.0.0.1:%d,127.0.0.1:%d,127.0.0.1:%d" % ports   # the headless DNS answer
run(options=[])                                     # default policy
run(options=[("grpc.lb_policy_name", "round_robin")])
run(options=[], stop_server_A_at_call=30)           # default policy, first pod dies
# look for: the default channel sends all 60 calls to one server despite knowing all three
# naive belief predicts: three addresses means three-way balancing, 20 / 20 / 20

Run on 22 Nov 2026 (grpcio 1.85.3, Python 3.14.6): pick_first gave A 60, round_robin gave 20 / 20 / 20, and killing A moved the remaining 30 calls to B alone. A headless Service fixes discovery, not balancing; the policy is a separate switch.

Measure it

  • See it: per-pod calls per second after a scale-out; balanced means new pods take a share within one re-resolution. grpcurl or channelz shows subchannels per channel: one means pick_first.
  • In production: max-to-median in-flight requests per pod, per service; well above 1 with zero errors means pinning. GPU or CPU utilisation variance across pods is the same signal in money.
  • Bounded by: a pinned pod → per-call balancing (L7, sidecar, round_robin). A fleet that never sees new pods → server MAX_CONNECTION_AGE forcing reconnects. Connection fan-out → a proxy tier instead of m·n client connections.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: HTTP/2 carries every call on one long-lived connection, and an L4 balancer such as kube-proxy chooses a backend once per connection, so a client's calls all land on one pod while the rest idle, with no errors anywhere. Fix it by deciding per call: an L7 proxy or mesh sidecar, or client-side balancing with a headless Service and round_robin, since gRPC's default pick_first does no balancing at all.

Q · Mechanism — Why doesn't HTTP/1.1 hit this? It isn't multiplexed: a client wanting concurrency opens a pool of connections, and each one gets its own balancing decision, so an L4 hop makes many decisions and spreads load acceptably. HTTP/2 deliberately collapses the pool to one connection because connections are expensive. The connection count was what the L4 hop distributed, so the protocol improvement and the balancing regression are the same change. Any multiplexed client hits it; gRPC just wears the name.

Q · Trade-off — Proxy, sidecar or client-side? A shared L7 tier keeps clients simple and policy central, at a hop and a shared failure domain. A sidecar gives per-call balancing with no client changes and a per-pod blast radius, at a proxy per pod. Client-side removes the hop but needs a competent policy in every language and costs m·n connections. The tipping point is who owns the clients: all yours in one or two languages favours client-side or proxyless xDS; anything else favours the proxy. The service mesh note owns the sidecar costs.

Q · Failure — You scaled from 40 to 60 pods and p99 didn't move. What's wrong? Distribution, not capacity. Confirm with per-pod request rate: twenty pods near zero, a few hot, error rate flat. Check how clients reach the service: a ClusterIP in front of gRPC, or a headless Service with a channel still on pick_first. Fix the path, then cap connection age so existing channels re-resolve and find the new pods; without that, long-lived clients ignore the scale-out until something breaks a connection.

Q · Design — A few gateway pods call forty GPU inference pods over gRPC, and request cost varies 10×. Where does the decision go? The binding constraint is utilisation of the most expensive resource, so the decision must be per call and load-aware. Put an Envoy hop on the gateway side, as a sidecar or a small routing tier, with endpoints from EndpointSlices and least-request picking, because round robin queues behind expensive calls (algorithms). Add slow start, since an empty new pod attracts least-request traffic before it's warm. The first signal to watch is max-to-median in-flight per pod. Model-aware routing lives in GPU inference load balancing; the service boundaries in microservice communication.

Compare

Fix Where the decision is made Cost Breaks when When you'd pick it
Shared L7 proxy a central Envoy or gateway tier one hop, a shared tier the tier saturates or fails heterogeneous or external clients
Mesh sidecar a proxy beside each client a proxy per pod the control plane lags you already run a mesh
Client-side round_robin the client's LB policy m·n connections, per-language config a language lacks the policy few languages, all clients yours
Proxyless xDS a control plane, applied in the client an xDS control plane clients lag the control plane big fleets wanting central policy, no hop
MAX_CONNECTION_AGE only nowhere: it re-rolls the L4 pick periodic reconnects load varies faster than the age you can't change the path yet

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Idle pods behind L4 ≥ 87.5% 5 client channels, 40 pods derived: above
Client-side connections m · n 5 × 40 = 200; 200 × 100 = 20,000 derived
Minimum gap between DNS re-resolutions 30 s gRPC C-core dns_min_time_between_resolutions_ms default (as of Nov 2026): gRPC channel args
pick_first, 3 addresses, 60 calls 60 / 0 / 0 grpcio 1.85.3, localhost measured: 22 Nov 2026
round_robin, same 20 / 20 / 20 same run measured: 22 Nov 2026
Envoy least-request sample size 2 hosts power of two choices, equal weights default (as of Nov 2026): Envoy docs

Pitfalls

  • "A Kubernetes Service balances gRPC like it balances HTTP/1.1"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the same Service spreads HTTP/1.1 traffic well, and gRPC is "just HTTP".
    ↳ Why it's wrong: kube-proxy picks per connection; HTTP/1.1 clients open many, a gRPC channel opens one and keeps it for hours.
    ↳ Think instead: an L4 hop balances connections, so count connections, not requests, before trusting it.
  • "A headless Service fixes it"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the client now sees every pod's address, which looks like the whole fix.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: gRPC's default pick_first sends every call to the first address that connects; the run above gave 60 / 0 / 0 with three addresses.
    ↳ Think instead: discovery and balancing are two switches: a headless Service plus a round_robin or xDS policy.
  • Not the same: connection balancing vs request balancing
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "load balancing", and dashboards rarely say which.
    ↳ Difference: connection balancing decides once per connection; request balancing decides per call or stream, which needs a hop that parses HTTP/2.
    ↳ Think instead: ask how many decisions per minute the hop makes; for one gRPC channel at L4 the answer is zero.
  • Don't fix a pin with a better hash or algorithm at L4.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: uneven load looks like a bad algorithm, and least-connections sounds smarter.
    ↳ What goes wrong: with five connections and forty pods, at least 35 pods idle whatever the algorithm; it's arithmetic.
    ↳ Do instead: move the decision to L7 or the client, and choose the algorithm there.
  • Don't add a mesh when a client setting would do.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the mesh fixes balancing for every service at once.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a control plane and a proxy per pod for one service whose clients you own.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler fix first: headless Service, round_robin and a connection age; adopt a mesh when you have other reasons for one.
  • Shelf life: the pinning arithmetic is permanent. Policy names, defaults and xDS support per language move.

Connections

Path:L4 vs L7algorithmsthe gRPC and HTTP/2 problemservice mesh
  • Builds on gRPC on HTTP/2: why every call shares one connection.
  • Owned elsewhere: gRPC in production owns connection age, deadlines and retry policy; Services and kube-proxy owns the L4 data path.
  • Bounded by outlier detection: per-call balancing still needs bad endpoints ejected.
  • Composes with headless Services: the discovery half of client-side balancing.
  • Decided in microservice communication: where the sync gRPC hop is chosen.

notes.title: Global Load Balancing — DNS, Anycast and Anycast Front Doors
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 4786: Operation of Anycast Services (BCP 126) · AWS: How Global Accelerator works · AWS: How Route 53 determines endpoint health · AWS: CreateEndpointGroup

TL;DR

Global load balancing picks the region before any regional balancer sees the request. DNS steering changes the answer, so failover waits on caches you don't control. Anycast keeps one address and moves the route, so there is no cache to wait out. An anycast front door adds health checks and weights on top, but holds open connections where they are.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:client resolves a nameDNS steering returns a region, cached for the TTL
or: client sends to one anycast IPBGP delivers it to the nearest edgeedge health checks pick a healthy regiona new connection follows any change

Recall

Prompt Answer
What bounds DNS failover? Detection + TTL + runtime caches + connection life: minutes, not the TTL.
What does anycast fail over on? A route withdrawal: no client, resolver or cached answer changes.
Global Accelerator and an unhealthy endpoint? Existing connections stay until idle timeout: 340 s TCP, 30 s UDP.

The idea

A payments API runs in two regions behind a DNS failover record with a 60 s TTL; the runbook promises one-minute failover. The primary dies. The check needs three failed rounds, resolvers hold the old answer, a JVM caches it, and pooled connections never re-resolve. In the caching sum, a similar cutover takes 17 minutes in the worst case.

With anycast, both regions' edges announce the same prefix. When one withdraws, routers send the next packet to the other, and the client's address stays correct. An anycast front door such as Global Accelerator does this on the provider's edge, then picks a healthy region per new connection.

The trade: DNS steering is cheap, works for any protocol and crosses providers, and you pay with failover bounded by other people's caches; anycast removes the cache, and you pay with one provider or your own BGP, plus flows that can move mid-connection.

How it works

The two entry points; purple is what you don't run.

DNS commits the client to one region until the caches let go; the edge can choose again per connection.

Rule What actually happens
DNS steering Weight, latency, geo and failover policies on the authoritative server, decided by the resolver's location; DNS load balancing owns the policies.
Health for DNS Route 53 checks every 10 or 30 s from many locations, and calls an endpoint unhealthy when 18% or fewer of checkers see it healthy.
Anycast One prefix announced from many sites; failover is a withdrawal. A route change mid-flow can reach another site and break TCP (anycast card).
Anycast front door Global Accelerator gives two static anycast IPv4 addresses, checks endpoints (30 s, 3 in a row by default), and applies traffic dials and weights.
Who in the middle acts on it The resolver for DNS; BGP routers and the provider's edge for anycast. With no healthy endpoint, Global Accelerator routes to all of them.

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): RFC 4786 (Dec 2006) set anycast operating practice; DNS steering and anycast front doors are standard managed services.
  • What won't change: a cached answer can't be recalled and a route change can't carry TCP state; every product picks between those limits.

On the wire

An illustrative endpoint group for a front door: region A takes 90% of its share, with the defaults written out (AWS CLI, flags per the API reference as of Nov 2026).

aws globalaccelerator create-endpoint-group \
  --listener-arn "$LISTENER" \
  --endpoint-group-region eu-west-1 \
  --traffic-dial-percentage 90 \
  --health-check-path /health/local \
  --health-check-interval-seconds 30 \
  --threshold-count 3 \
  --endpoint-configurations EndpointId="$ALB_ARN"
# --traffic-dial-percentage: the rest spills to other regions' groups
# --health-check-interval-seconds: 10 or 30 only; 30 is the default
# --threshold-count: default 3, both to mark unhealthy and to restore
# the default that bites: an open TCP connection keeps its endpoint until 340 s idle

Measure it

  • See it: dig +short against two public resolvers during a DNS failover shows them disagreeing until each TTL expires; an anycast address answers from a different site after a withdrawal.
  • In production: per region, request share against intended weights; per failover, time until the last request reaches the dead region.
  • Bounded by: a dead region still getting traffic → anycast or a front door for seconds-scale moves, and short connection lifetimes so old flows re-pick.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Global balancing picks the region. DNS steering changes the answer, so failover is detection plus TTL plus runtime caches plus connection life: minutes, and it crosses providers. Anycast keeps one address and moves the route, so there's no cache term. A front door like Global Accelerator adds health checks, weights and dials, but holds open TCP connections until 340 s idle.

Q · Mechanism — Why is anycast failover faster than DNS failover? Nothing on the client side has to change. Every site announces the same prefix, and routers forward to the nearest announcement. When a site withdraws, routing converges and the next packet goes elsewhere, while the client's cached address stays valid. DNS failover must reach each client through caches you don't control, each on its own clock, which TTL and caching layers adds up.

Q · Trade-off — DNS steering or an anycast front door for a multi-region API? DNS when minutes are acceptable, the regions span providers, or you need per-country policy: a record change is the only lever that crosses providers. A front door when failover must take seconds or you want two fixed IPs for allow-lists: it removes the cache term but ties you to one edge network. The usual layering is anycast at the edge for absorption and fast moves, with DNS weights behind it for regional origins.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Route 53 health check interval 10 or 30 s unhealthy at ≤18% of checkers healthy default (as of Nov 2026): Route 53 docs
Global Accelerator checks 30 s, threshold 3 interval 10 or 30 only default (as of Nov 2026): GA API reference
GA idle timeout 340 s TCP · 30 s UDP open flows keep their endpoint until then default (as of Nov 2026): GA docs
GA detection 60–90 s (T−1)·I … T·I = 2·30 … 3·30 derived

Pitfalls

  • "A 60-second TTL means a 60-second failover"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the TTL is the one number you set.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: failover adds detection, runtime timers and pooled connections that never re-resolve; the worked sum reaches 17 minutes.
    ↳ Think instead: the TTL is one term of a sum, and the largest term is often connection life.
  • Not the same: anycast vs an anycast front door
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both give one address from many places.
    ↳ Difference: plain anycast is routing, so a route change can move a flow and break TCP. A front door terminates or tracks the flow at its edge, keeps it on one endpoint, and re-picks only for new connections.
    ↳ Think instead: routing moves packets; a front door moves connections.
  • "Marking a region unhealthy moves its traffic now"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the health flag flips at once.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: Global Accelerator keeps existing connections on an endpoint until the idle timeout, even if it is unhealthy or removed; a busy long-lived connection never goes idle.
    ↳ Think instead: failover moves new connections; cap connection age so old ones re-pick.
  • Don't buy a global balancer when one region and DNS would do.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: "multi-region" sounds like the grown-up architecture.
    ↳ What goes wrong: routing is the easy half; two regions writing one dataset is the hard half, and it isn't a networking problem.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option, a DNS failover record to a warm standby, until a recovery target forces more.
  • Shelf life: cache and routing limits are durable; product defaults change.

Connections

Path:outlier detectionglobal load balancingCDN and edge
  • Builds on DNS load balancing: the policies DNS steering applies.
  • Owned elsewhere: TTL and caching layers owns the failover sum; the anycast card owns anycast's mechanism.
  • Composes with health checks: the same depth rules decide which region is healthy.
  • Contrasts with CDN and edge: an anycast edge that also caches.
  • Decided in resilience patterns: where a service chooses its failover target.

notes.title: API Gateway — Identity-Aware Policy Before the Service
notes.html:
References

Envoy: JWT authentication filter · AWS: ALB user authentication · Gateway API: Introduction

TL;DR

An API gateway is a reverse proxy that knows who is calling. It validates the credential, checks the caller may use this route, counts quota per tenant, then routes. Identity is the line: a load balancer picks an instance, a gateway decides whether this caller gets in at all.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:bearer tokenverify signature, iss, aud, exp401 if badroute allowed for this caller?403 if nottenant quota429 + Retry-After if overroute to the service

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does a gateway have that a load balancer doesn't? The caller's identity, so policy is keyed on tenant, not IP.
Why must auth come before quota? The quota is counted per tenant, and the tenant is known only after auth.
Envoy jwt_authn with no audiences set? It doesn't check aud; any token from that issuer passes.

The idea

A B2B API rate-limits at the edge: 100 requests a minute per IP. One customer's 400 engineers sit behind a corporate NAT and share one address, so they hit 429 all morning. Meanwhile a scraper spread across 2,000 addresses never comes near the limit. The limit is keyed on the only thing the edge knows, an address, and an address is neither a customer nor an attacker.

Behind authentication the limit keys on the tenant in the token: the NAT'd customer gets its quota, and the scraper gets 401 or burns one revocable key.

The trade: a gateway turns policy into per-caller policy, and you pay with a credential check on every request, a quota store the gateway now depends on, and a hop that business logic will try to move into.

How it works

The checks run in the only order that works; each rejection is cheaper than the next stage.

A rejection never costs a backend connection.

Rule What actually happens
Credential Signature, issuer, audience and time checks against cached keys (JWKS). API authentication owns which mechanism to use.
Quota Counted per tenant across all gateway replicas; per-replica counters drift under uneven balancing (rate limiting owns the algorithms).
Transformation Header injection (tenant ID, claims) and version routing are gateway work. Joining responses from several services is application code.
The middle The service now trusts the gateway's headers, so it must accept traffic only from the gateway, or verify the forwarded token itself.

Evolution

  • Maturity today: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026). Managed balancers absorbed gateway features: an ALB authenticates users through OIDC or Cognito on HTTPS listeners and passes a signed x-amzn-oidc-data header.
  • Changed by Kubernetes Gateway API: a name collision. It's resources that model cluster routing; its docs say some API gateways can be programmed through it.
  • What's next and what won't change: gateways for model and agent traffic add per-token quotas and model routing. The line stays: policy that needs identity goes behind the credential check.

On the wire

Envoy's JWT filter, adapted from its docs; both comments mark defaults that let traffic through.

providers:
  idp:
    issuer: https://auth.example.com
    audiences: [orders-api]          # omit this and any token from the issuer passes, for any API
    remote_jwks:
      http_uri:
        uri: https://auth.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json
        cluster: idp_jwks            # a cluster to reach the IdP; key fetches go through it
        timeout: 1s
      cache_duration: 300s           # keys cached; a rotated key needs this long to arrive
    forward_payload_header: x-jwt-payload   # the service reads claims, never re-parses the token
rules:
- match: { prefix: /health }         # no requires: verification skipped
- match: { prefix: / }
  requires: { provider_name: idp }   # a path matching no rule is NOT verified: keep this catch-all last

By default the filter also reads a token from the access_token query parameter, which puts credentials in access logs; set from_headers to read only Authorization.

Measure it

  • See it: curl -i with no token, a wrong-audience token and past quota shows 401, 401, 429 + Retry-After, in the gateway's log and never the service's.
  • In production: per tenant and route, rejections split into 401, 403 and 429; gateway-added latency (total minus upstream time); JWKS fetch failures; quota-store latency.
  • Bounded by: the quota store going down → a written fail-open or fail-closed rule per route. The IdP's key endpoint going down → cached keys (cache_duration) carry the gateway through.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A gateway is the hop that knows who is calling. Underneath it's a reverse proxy, usually Envoy or nginx. On top it validates the token, checks the route against the caller's permissions, counts the tenant's quota and routes. Everything is keyed on identity, which is why it sits behind the load balancer and in front of services. The anti-pattern is business logic: joins and field mapping belong in a service.

Q · Mechanism — Where does the load balancer end and the gateway begin? At identity. The load balancer chooses an instance using what the connection and request line give it. The gateway decides whether this caller may make this call at this rate, which needs a validated credential. So the balancer gets the request to a healthy gateway replica, and the gateway applies per-tenant policy. Managed products blur the line (an ALB with OIDC does gateway work), so in a design discussion ask where identity is established. Per-tenant policy is possible only after that point.

Q · Trade-off — A dedicated gateway tier, or auth filters in the ingress controller? Filters in the ingress remove a hop and a component, and modern ingress controllers run JWT checks and limits. For one team that's enough. A dedicated tier earns its place when policy ownership splits, so product teams can change quotas without editing the cluster's ingress, or when you need state the ingress doesn't keep: API keys, per-tenant quota counters, developer onboarding. My tipping point is a second team that must change policy independently.

Compare

Component Decides Knows the caller? Typical traffic When you'd pick it
L7 load balancer which instance no (unless it authenticates) north–south always, underneath
API gateway whether this caller gets in, at what rate yes, from the token north–south, external or multi-tenant public or partner APIs with quotas
Ingress / Gateway API which Service, by host and path only with an auth filter north–south into a cluster Kubernetes exposure (ingress controllers)

Pitfalls

  • Not the same: API gateway vs Kubernetes Gateway API
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: the names differ by one word, and both sit at the cluster edge.
    ↳ Difference: an API gateway enforces identity-aware policy; Gateway API is Kubernetes resources (Gateway, HTTPRoute) that describe routing.
    ↳ Think instead: Gateway API is how you configure a proxy; an API gateway is what the proxy does, if it validates callers.
  • "Rate limiting belongs at the edge, as far out as possible"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: rejecting early saves work, and DDoS advice says to filter at the edge.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: before authentication the only key is the IP, which over-limits a whole company behind one NAT and barely slows an attacker on many addresses.
    ↳ Think instead: volumetric protection at the edge, quota behind auth, where the tenant is known.
  • Don't put business logic in the gateway.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: one response joined from three services, or a renamed field, is a few lines of gateway config.
    ↳ What goes wrong: service contracts end up encoded in config a platform team deploys on its own schedule, so every product change waits on that team.
    ↳ Do instead: keep transformation to headers and versions; put composition in a small backend service its own team owns.
  • Don't add a gateway for one team and five services.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it looks like the grown-up diagram.
    ↳ What goes wrong: another hop, failure domain and config language, for checks an ingress auth filter or the ALB's OIDC action already does.
    ↳ Do instead: start there; add a gateway for a second team or per-tenant quota.
  • Shelf life: the identity line is durable. Managed quotas, timeouts and the features balancers absorb change often.

Connections

Path:reverse proxy responsibilitiesAPI gatewayingress controllersservice mesh
  • Builds on reverse proxy responsibilities: the same pipeline, with identity added before quota.
  • Owned elsewhere: rate limiting owns the algorithms and distributed counting; API authentication owns the credential choice.
  • Contrasts with service mesh: east–west policy by workload identity, not caller identity.
  • Decided in communication patterns: the gateway pattern in a service design.
  • Drilled in where is the gateway: placing it and naming what it owns.

notes.title: Ingress Controllers and the Gateway API — Kubernetes' Front Door
notes.html:
References

Kubernetes: Ingress (frozen) · Gateway API: Introduction · Kubernetes blog: Ingress NGINX retirement (11 Nov 2025) · Gateway API v1.7.0 release notes

TL;DR

An Ingress or a Gateway API route is configuration with no behaviour of its own: a controller watches it and programs a reverse proxy (Envoy, nginx, HAProxy) that does the work. Ingress standardised only host and path, so everything else became unvalidated vendor annotations. The Gateway API types those features and splits them across three roles; Ingress is frozen and its most-used controller, ingress-nginx, is retired.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:cloud L4 LBcontroller's proxy podsTLS ends, host and path matchedEndpointSlice lookuppod IP
platform team owns Gatewayapp team attaches HTTPRoutecontroller compiles bothproxy config updated

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does an Ingress do with no controller installed? Nothing: it's stored config; no proxy reads it.
The three Gateway API resources and owners? GatewayClass (infra provider), Gateway (cluster operator), Routes (app developer).
ingress-nginx status, Nov 2026? Retired: maintenance ended March 2026, repo archived, no security fixes.

The idea

A team applies an Ingress for a streaming endpoint with nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-buffering: "off" misspelled. Nothing errors: annotations are free-form strings, unknown keys are ignored, and responses stay buffered until users report frozen token streams. A 10% canary has no Ingress field either, so it's another vendor annotation, and switching controllers means rewriting them all.

The Gateway API makes those features typed fields that the API server validates: header matches, weighted backendRefs, retries, mirroring. It splits ownership: a platform team owns the Gateway (listeners, TLS certificates, which namespaces may attach), and app teams own their HTTPRoutes without cluster-wide rights.

The trade: typed, portable, role-split routing costs a migration and a second model to learn while both APIs run; staying on Ingress costs vendor lock-in through annotations and, on ingress-nginx, an unpatched proxy at the edge.

How it works

Rule What actually happens
Two halves The controller is a control loop that watches resources and writes proxy config; the proxy is the data plane. If the controller dies, the proxy keeps serving its last config: routing freezes, traffic flows.
The entry point A cloud L4 load balancer points at the controller's own LoadBalancer Service; the Ingress isn't in the packet path.
The middle The proxy ends TLS and matches routes. Sending to pod IPs from EndpointSlices keeps the balancing decision per request; sending to the ClusterIP hands it to kube-proxy, per connection.
Config changes nginx applies a change by starting new workers; old ones finish existing connections, so WebSockets hold old workers until worker_shutdown_timeout cuts them. Envoy-based controllers push updates over xDS without restarting workers.

Evolution

Lineage:2020 Ingress GA (Kubernetes 1.19)2023 Gateway API v1.02024 GRPCRoute and mesh GA (v1.1)2026 TLSRoute, TCPRoute, UDPRoute GA (v1.5, v1.6)Oct 2026 HTTPRoute retries Standard (v1.7)
  • Maturity today: 🟡 Maturing, Nov 2026. Gateway API v1.7.0 shipped 29 Oct 2026; core routing is GA, and features still graduate each release.
  • Changed in Kubernetes: Ingress is frozen: GA and staying, but with no new features; the project recommends Gateway. Ingress NGINX was retired in March 2026; existing installs run unpatched.
  • What's next and what won't change: policy attachment and inference routing move; the control-loop and data-plane split stays.

On the wire

Illustrative HTTPRoute: each field here was an annotation, or impossible, on Ingress.

apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata: { name: chat, namespace: chat-team }    # app team's namespace, app team's object
spec:
  parentRefs: [{ name: edge, namespace: infra }]   # the platform team's Gateway; it must allow this namespace
  hostnames: ["chat.example.com"]
  rules:
  - matches: [{ path: { type: PathPrefix, value: /v1 } }]
    backendRefs:
    - { name: chat-v1, port: 8080, weight: 90 }    # typed canary split, validated by the API server
    - { name: chat-v2, port: 8080, weight: 10 }
    retry: { codes: [503], attempts: 2 }           # Standard channel since v1.7 (Oct 2026)

Measure it

  • See it: kubectl get httproute chat -o yaml shows status.parents[].conditions: Accepted and ResolvedRefs true means the controller took it; an Ingress has no equivalent, so a typo shows only in traffic.
  • In production: per route, request rate and 5xx at the proxy; config-sync lag between apply and live; old-worker count or connection resets after each config change.
  • Bounded by: a dead control loop → the proxy serves last-known config; alert on sync lag. Reload churn → an xDS-based controller. An unpatched edge → a maintained controller.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: An ingress controller is a reverse proxy in the cluster plus a control loop that turns Kubernetes resources into its config. Ingress standardised only host and path, so real features became unvalidated vendor annotations. The Gateway API replaces it with typed routes and three roles: the platform team owns the Gateway, app teams own routes. Ingress is frozen, and ingress-nginx was retired in March 2026.

Q · Mechanism — Trace an external request to a pod. A cloud L4 load balancer forwards to one of the controller's proxy pods. The proxy ends TLS with a certificate from a Secret, matches host and path against config compiled from every route, and sends straight to a pod IP from the Service's EndpointSlices. The detail worth checking: a controller that sends to the ClusterIP instead puts kube-proxy's per-connection pick behind the L7 hop, which pins HTTP/2 (the gRPC problem).

Q · Trade-off — Stay on Ingress or migrate? New clusters start on the Gateway API: Ingress gets no new features and the role split matters as soon as two teams share an entry point. For an existing cluster the trigger is the annotation surface, not the feature list: several teams editing one Ingress, or a controller swap blocked by vendor annotations. On ingress-nginx there's no choice left, because the controller gets no security fixes. ingress2gateway (v1.2.0, Jul 2026) converts manifests and some provider annotations; review the rest by hand.

Compare

Routing in the spec Everything else Ownership When you'd pick it
Ingress host and path vendor annotations, unvalidated one object, one permission an existing, simple cluster on a maintained controller
Gateway API host, path, header, method, query; weights; gRPC, TLS, TCP, UDP; mesh routes on a Service typed fields and policies GatewayClass, Gateway, Route split by role new clusters, shared entry points, anything past host and path

Pitfalls

  • "I applied the Ingress, so routing is configured"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: kubectl apply succeeds and kubectl get ingress lists it.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the API server stores it; only a running controller whose class matches acts on it, and a misspelled annotation is silently ignored.
    ↳ Think instead: config isn't behaviour: check the controller's logs, or on Gateway API the route's Accepted condition.
  • Not the same: the Gateway API vs an API gateway
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: almost the same name, and both sit at the edge.
    ↳ Difference: the Gateway API is a Kubernetes routing spec many proxies implement; an API gateway is a product adding auth, quotas and keys per consumer.
    ↳ Think instead: a spec for routing vs a product for API consumers; the API gateway note owns the second.
  • Don't route east–west traffic out through the ingress.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the ingress already has TLS, routing and logs, so internal callers use its public name.
    ↳ What goes wrong: calls leave and re-enter the cluster: extra hops, a shared failure domain, and LB bills for traffic that never needed to leave.
    ↳ Do instead: call the Service directly, or use a mesh route (service mesh).
  • Don't stay on a retired controller because it still works.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: existing ingress-nginx installs keep serving, and migration is work with no new feature.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the most exposed proxy in the cluster stops getting security fixes, so the next CVE has no patch.
    ↳ Do instead: plan the move to a maintained controller, preferably on the Gateway API.
  • Shelf life: controller status and which features are Standard change every release; re-check every three months.

Connections

Path:API gatewayingress controllersservice mesh
  • Builds on reverse proxy responsibilities: the controller's data plane is one.
  • Owned elsewhere: ingress, gateway and mesh in Kubernetes owns the cluster view; buffering vs streaming owns the streaming setting.
  • Contrasts with API gateway: per-consumer auth and quotas, not cluster routing.
  • Composes with Services and kube-proxy: the L4 layer under the backends.

notes.title: Service Mesh — Sidecar vs Ambient, and When It's Worth It
notes.html:
References

Istio: Sidecar or ambient? · Istio: Ambient mode overview · Linkerd: Load balancing · Kubernetes: Sidecar containers

TL;DR

A mesh moves mTLS, retries, timeouts, per-request balancing and telemetry out of every service and into proxies that carry all service-to-service traffic, changed by config instead of a library upgrade per language. Sidecar mode puts a full proxy in every pod; ambient mode puts an L4 proxy on every node and adds an L7 proxy only where you ask for one. You pay a hop on every internal call and a control plane that becomes critical.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:app dials b as usualredirect rules send it to the local proxyproxy picks a B podmTLS to B's proxyplain HTTP to B on loopback
ambient: appnode's ztunnelwaypoint (L7, optional)B's ztunnelB

Recall

Prompt Answer
Ambient's two layers? ztunnel per node for mTLS and L4; waypoint per namespace for L7.
Does ztunnel alone balance gRPC per request? No: L4 balances connections only; per-request needs a waypoint.
Kubernetes fix for sidecar start and stop order? Native sidecars: initContainers with restartPolicy: Always, stable in 1.33.

The idea

A platform runs services in Go, Python and Java and must encrypt all internal traffic for an audit. With libraries, that's three mTLS implementations, three retry policies drifting apart, and a certificate-rotation project per language. Internal gRPC is also pinned, one pod hot per caller (the gRPC problem).

A mesh intercepts each call at a proxy the platform team controls. The proxy gets a workload certificate from the control plane, speaks mTLS to the destination's proxy, balances each request across B's pods, and reports the same metrics for every language.
