Ambient mode makes the price proportional: every pod gets mTLS from the node's ztunnel, and only namespaces that need L7 policy get a waypoint.

The trade: uniform security and traffic policy across languages, paid for with a proxy hop on every internal call, proxy CPU and memory, and a control plane whose outage freezes certificates and config everywhere.

How it works

One logical call in sidecar mode; ambient replaces both proxies with node ztunnels and at most one waypoint.

Policy lives in the proxies, so it's the same for every language and changes without a deploy.

Rule What actually happens
Interception An init container or CNI plugin redirects the pod's traffic through the proxy; the app dials the same address it always did.
Identity The control plane issues and rotates workload certificates; a sidecar holds only its pod's keys, a ztunnel holds keys for every workload on its node.
Ambient split ztunnel does mTLS, L4 authorisation, TCP metrics and connection-level balancing; a waypoint (an Envoy per namespace) adds retries, routing, per-request balancing and L7 metrics.
The middle The control plane pushes config and certificates. If it's down, proxies keep their last config, but new workloads, config and certificates wait.

The per-call cost lands hardest on the fastest calls, using Istio's own latency figures:

sidecar mode, per call:  0.63–0.88 ms (p90–p99)   ← both proxies, Istio's measurement
ambient: ztunnel 0.16–0.20 ms, waypoint 0.40–0.50 ms
5 serial internal calls, sidecar p99 ≈ 5 × 0.88 ≈ 4.4 ms   ← adds per hop
on a 2 ms cache call: 0.88 / 2 ≈ 44% more; on a 40 ms call ≈ 2%

Evolution

  • Maturity today: 🟡 Maturing, Nov 2026. Sidecar meshes are long settled; Istio's ambient mode went GA in 1.24 (7 Nov 2024), single-cluster only in Istio's own comparison, and Istio 1.32.0 shipped 9 Nov 2026.
  • Changed in Kubernetes 1.33: native sidecar containers are stable. The kubelet starts them before the app and stops them after it, which removes the classic startup race and the Job that never finishes because its sidecar won't exit.
  • What's next and what won't change: mesh routing converges on the Gateway API (mesh support GA in v1.1, May 2024). Per-request behaviour still needs an L7 proxy.

On the wire

Illustrative Istio ambient enrolment, run against a cluster: L4 first, L7 only where needed.

kubectl label namespace chat istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient   # ztunnel mTLS for every pod, no sidecar injection
istioctl waypoint apply -n chat                                 # deploys an Envoy waypoint for this namespace
kubectl label namespace chat istio.io/use-waypoint=waypoint     # chat's services now get L7: retries, per-request LB

Without the last two lines, gRPC into chat is encrypted but balanced per connection.

Measure it

  • See it: istioctl ztunnel-config workloads lists which pods ztunnel captures; correct is every enrolled pod with HBONE protocol. In sidecar mode, istioctl proxy-status shows each proxy SYNCED.
  • In production: per hop, p99 added by proxies; proxy CPU and memory per pod or node; config push latency from the control plane; certificate expiry headroom per workload.
  • Bounded by: a control-plane outage → proxies run on last config; alert on push lag and certificate age. Proxy overhead on hot paths → ambient L4 only, or no waypoint there.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A mesh puts a proxy in front of every service, per pod in sidecar mode or per node in ambient mode, and moves mTLS, retries, timeouts, per-request balancing and telemetry there, so policy is the same in every language and changes by config. The cost is latency per internal call, proxy resources and a critical control plane, so the real question is the threshold where it pays.

Q · Mechanism — What changes on the wire when a pod joins the mesh? Redirect rules send its traffic to a proxy instead of the destination. The proxy terminates the connection, picks a destination pod, and opens mTLS to the other side's proxy with a certificate from the control plane; that proxy delivers plain traffic over loopback. In ambient mode the node's ztunnel carries it over HBONE (HTTP/2 CONNECT inside mTLS on port 15008), and a waypoint joins only for L7 policy, so without one, balancing stays per connection.

Q · Trade-off — When is a mesh worth it? When there's a requirement you can't meet otherwise: mTLS everywhere across a polyglot estate, or per-request balancing of internal gRPC without touching clients. One language and a dozen services is better served by one good library with no hop and no control plane. Prefer ambient where the platform supports it, because most pods need only L4 encryption. Observability alone is the weakest reason; libraries and eBPF tools give it more cheaply.

Pitfalls

  • "A mesh gives us zero trust"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: mTLS and workload identity are on every slide about zero trust.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: mTLS authenticates the caller and encrypts the call; whether A should call B is an authorisation policy nobody wrote yet.
    ↳ Think instead: identity is the input; deny-by-default authorisation policy is the control. See mTLS.
  • Not the same: ambient's ztunnel vs a waypoint
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "the ambient proxy", and enrolling a namespace looks like joining the mesh.
    ↳ Difference: ztunnel is L4 per node, with mTLS and connection-level balancing only; a waypoint is the L7 Envoy that balances per request.
    ↳ Think instead: gRPC still pins under ztunnel alone; add a waypoint where per-request behaviour matters.
  • "The sidecar is transparent to the application"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: no code changes, and the app dials the same address.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: transparent to code, not to lifecycle or timeouts: an app that dials before its proxy is ready fails, and a proxy timeout shorter than the app's fires first.
    ↳ Think instead: two components in one pod: use native sidecars for ordering and align timeouts in both.
  • Don't adopt a mesh for observability alone.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: uniform metrics and traces with no code change.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every internal call pays proxy latency and every pod or node pays proxy resources for something cheaper elsewhere.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: OpenTelemetry libraries or eBPF-based tooling, and a mesh when mTLS or gRPC balancing demands it.
  • Shelf life: ambient's limits and the latency figures change by release; re-check every three months.

Connections

Path:ingress controllersservice meshCDN and edge
  • Builds on the gRPC problem: a mesh fixes it at L7 without client changes.
  • Owned elsewhere: outlier detection owns ejection and breakers; ingress, gateway and mesh owns the cluster view.
  • Composes with mTLS: the identity mechanism the mesh automates.
  • Bounded by tail latency: proxy hops add up across a fan-out.

notes.title: CDN & Edge — PoPs, Shields, Cache Keys, Purge
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9111: HTTP Caching · 📜 RFC 9213: Targeted HTTP Cache Control · CloudFront: the cache key · Cloudflare: cache keys

TL;DR

A CDN is a reverse-proxy tier at many points of presence: TLS ends near the user, and each PoP keeps a cache in front of a shield tier and your origin. Correctness and hit ratio are both decided by the cache key, the request parts that make two requests "the same object". Purge is how you take a wrong object back out of every PoP.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:GET /products?page=2nearest PoP, TLS ends therekey = host + path + chosen query, headershit? serveshield: one fetch for all PoPsoriginstored per Cache-Control, or CDN-Cache-Control

Recall

Prompt Answer
Query string in the default key: Cloudflare vs CloudFront CachingOptimized? Cloudflare: included. CloudFront: excluded.
Which header sets CDN policy without touching browsers? CDN-Cache-Control (RFC 9213, Jun 2022).
What does a shield tier save? Many PoP misses become one origin fetch per object.

The idea

A shop adds utm_source to every newsletter link. On a CDN whose default key includes the full query string, each campaign tag is a separate object, so the origin takes the launch traffic. The team switches to a policy that drops query strings, and now everyone gets the cached page 1 for /products?page=2. Both mistakes are about the key, not the TTL.

The fix is an allow-list: the key includes page and nothing else from the query. RFC 9111 §2 sets the minimum key, method plus target URI and Vary; the rest is CDN configuration with a different default per CDN. HTTP caching owns freshness, Vary and versioned URLs; this note owns where the caches sit and what they key on.

The trade: every request part in the key makes the cache more correct and less effective; the key lists exactly the parts that change the body.

How it works

A miss at two PoPs reaches the origin once, because both go through the shield.

The shield turns a fleet of cold PoPs into one origin request per object; the PoP shortens every connection, cached or not.

Rule What actually happens
Default key differs by CDN Cloudflare: scheme, host, path, full query, Origin. CloudFront: distribution domain and path; CachingOptimized adds only normalised Accept-Encoding (as of Nov 2026).
Default cacheability differs too Cloudflare caches by file extension and "does not cache HTML or JSON by default"; CloudFront without a policy defaults to a 24 h TTL.
Targeted policy CDN-Cache-Control: max-age=60 binds CDNs only; browsers still read Cache-Control. CDNs typically forward it downstream and MAY strip it (RFC 9213 §3).
Purge an API call fanned out to every PoP: by URL, tag, prefix, host or everything (Cloudflare); rate limited, and a variant outside the purged key survives.
Edge compute and signed URLs code at the PoP (Workers, CloudFront Functions) rewrites keys or personalises; a signed URL lets the edge serve private objects without asking your origin.

Evolution

  • Maturity today: 🟢 Established, Nov 2026. RFC 9111 (Jun 2022) is the caching contract; every major CDN keys, shields and purges.
  • Changed in RFC 9213: CDN policy no longer has to be smuggled into s-maxage or a vendor header; one standard field targets CDNs.
  • What's next and what won't change: more edge logic, finer purge. The CDN still can't know which request parts change your body.

On the wire

Break it: one edge cache, 1,000 requests for /products?page=1–3&utm_source=mail1–500, three key policies. A model run locally; the origin's body depends on page only.

policies = {"full URL": lambda u: u,                       # Cloudflare's default shape
            "path only": lambda u: urlsplit(u).path,        # CachingOptimized's shape
            "allow-list page": lambda u: (path(u), q(u)["page"])}
# look for: origin fetches and wrong pages served, per policy
# naive belief predicts: dropping the query only raises the hit ratio

Python 3.15: full URL fetched from the origin 727 times, 0 wrong pages; path only fetched once and served 656 wrong pages; the allow-list fetched 3 times, 0 wrong. One key decides both.

Measure it

  • See it: curl -sI twice; the cache-status header (cf-cache-status, x-cache, RFC 9211 Cache-Status) goes MISS then HIT. Change one query parameter: does it miss?
  • In production: per route, edge hit ratio and origin requests per user request; distinct keys per path. Keys per path growing with traffic means fragmentation.
  • Bounded by: a wrong object served to many users → an allow-listed key, private on personal responses, a tested purge; an origin stampede at expiry → shield tier plus request collapsing.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A CDN puts reverse proxies at many PoPs, so TLS ends close to the user and a cache sits in front of a shield and your origin. Everything that matters is the cache key: include a part that doesn't change the body and you fragment the cache; leave out one that does and you serve one user's page to another. Purge pulls a bad object back; hashed URLs avoid needing it.

Q · Mechanism — What happens on a miss, and why doesn't a cold launch flatten the origin? The PoP misses and asks its shield, a regional cache tier (CloudFront Origin Shield, Cloudflare Tiered Cache). The shield misses once and fetches once, and inside one data center concurrent misses for the same key wait on a single fetch (Cloudflare calls it a cache lock). So a hundred cold PoPs make one origin request per object, not a hundred.

Q · Trade-off — Long TTL plus purge, or short TTL? Short TTLs fix themselves, but every expiry is an origin revalidation, forever. Long TTL plus purge keeps origin load near zero, but correctness then rests on a rate-limited fan-out reaching every PoP and variant. For assets, neither: hashed URLs never need purging. Purge is for pages you must change on demand; the tipping point is whether the URL can change when the content does.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
CloudFront CachingOptimized TTLs min 1 s · default 86,400 s · max 31,536,000 s managed policy default (as of Nov 2026): AWS docs
CloudFront origin response timeout 30 s first byte, and between packets default (as of Nov 2026): AWS docs
Shielded origin fetches 1 per object, not 1 per PoP P cold PoPs → P fetches without a shield derived

Pitfalls

  • Not the same: the cache key vs Vary
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both decide which stored response a request gets.
    ↳ Difference: Vary is the origin's per-response instruction under RFC 9111 §4.1; the key policy is CDN configuration applied before Vary, and it can drop a query part the origin depends on.
    ↳ Think instead: the CDN's key first, Vary on top; check both when a page is wrong.
  • Don't let a personalised response be cacheable by default.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the route returned JSON and Cloudflare doesn't cache JSON by default.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a "cache everything" rule or another CDN's defaults stores it, and one user's account page reaches everyone at that PoP.
    ↳ Do instead: Cache-Control: private or no-store on anything per user, set at the origin.
  • "A CDN only helps static content"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: hit ratio is the headline metric, and dynamic responses never hit.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: TCP and TLS end at the nearby PoP, and the PoP reuses a warm connection to origin, so uncacheable requests save handshake round trips too.
    ↳ Think instead: the edge shortens every connection; the cache only helps repeats.
  • Don't put a caching CDN route in front of a token stream.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: one distribution for the whole site is simpler.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the edge may buffer, or time out between packets, so the stream arrives late or cut.
    ↳ Do instead: a stream route with caching off and buffering off, per buffering vs streaming proxies.
  • Shelf life: RFC 9111 and RFC 9213 are stable. Default keys, TTLs and purge limits are vendor facts; re-check every 3 months.

Connections

Path:reverse proxy responsibilitiesglobal load balancingCDN and edgebuffering vs streaming proxies
  • Builds on reverse proxy responsibilities: a CDN is that list, run at many PoPs.
  • Owned elsewhere: HTTP caching owns freshness, Vary, s-maxage and hashed URLs.
  • Builds on global load balancing: anycast and DNS steer users to the nearest PoP.
  • Composes with WAF, DDoS and bot mitigation: they run at the same edge hop.
  • Decided in URL shortener: a read-heavy redirect path where the edge carries most traffic.

TL;DR

A buffering proxy reads the upstream response into its own memory and forwards it later; a streaming proxy forwards each chunk as it arrives. For a page that's the same thing, and buffering protects your backend from slow clients. For a stream it turns time to first token into total generation time, with the same status, bytes and duration, so no dashboard notices. The second, separate failure is an idle or total timeout on some hop that cuts a stream which started fine.

The idea

Your chat demo streams beautifully against the app server. Behind production nginx, users stare at a spinner for eight seconds and then the whole answer lands at once. The status is 200, the error rate is zero, the origin's own time to first byte is 200 ms. Nothing failed; a hop held the bytes. nginx buffers proxied responses by default, and a short token stream never fills its buffers, so nginx keeps it until the origin closes.

Buffering exists for a good reason. With it on, nginx "receives a response from the proxied server as soon as possible" into its buffers, so the backend's worker is free while nginx dribbles the bytes to a phone on a bad link. With it off, "the response is passed to a client synchronously, immediately as it is received" (nginx docs). That's right for a stream and wrong for a large download to slow clients.

So the fix is per route: stream routes don't buffer and don't compress, and every timeout on the path is set above the longest silence the stream can have. A heartbeat comment keeps that silence short.

The trade: buffering buys backend protection from slow clients and costs every byte's timing; streaming buys first-token latency and costs a backend connection held for the stream's whole life.

The same ten-token stream through one hop, two settings.

Both runs deliver the same bytes in the same total time; only the first byte moves, which is why no server-side metric sees it.

On the wire

🧾 Command first: two location blocks, so only the stream route gives up buffering.

location /api/ {
    proxy_pass http://app;              # defaults: buffering on, protects workers from slow clients
}
location /api/stream/ {
    proxy_pass http://app;
    proxy_buffering off;                # forward each chunk as it arrives
    gzip off;                           # a compressor batches small writes
    proxy_read_timeout 300s;            # gap between reads, above the longest silence
}

The origin can opt out per response with X-Accel-Buffering: no unless proxy_ignore_headers drops it. From outside the edge, curl -N shows which hop holds the bytes:

curl -sN -o /dev/null -w 'first byte %{time_starttransfer}s  total %{time_total}s\n' https://edge.example/api/stream/
# first byte ≈ total → some hop buffers. Repeat hop by hop, origin first, until the gap appears.

Break it: an SSE origin on 127.0.0.1 sending 10 events 200 ms apart, read directly and through three proxies of our own.

modes = {"direct": origin, "stream": forward_each_chunk,
         "buffer": hold_until_upstream_closes, "threshold": flush_at_8192_bytes}
for name, hop in modes.items():
    first, total, events = client(hop)          # time to first `data:` line, end, count
# then: a streaming proxy with a 1 s read timeout, origin silent for 1.5 s
# look for: same total and same 10 events everywhere, first event 200 ms vs 2 s
# naive belief predicts: a bigger 8 KB buffer flushes early, so first event stays near 200 ms

Python 3.15, run twice: direct and streaming saw the first event at 200–204 ms; buffering and the 8 KB threshold both at 2,023–2,037 ms, with all 10 events and the same total. The stream is 160 bytes, so a size threshold never fires. The 1 s read timeout closed the slow stream at 1,001 ms with 0 of 3 events delivered after the headers.

Measure it

  • See it: curl -N -w '%{time_starttransfer} %{time_total}' through each hop in turn; correct is first byte near the origin's first token, far below total.
  • In production: per stream route, client-side time to first byte divided by origin-side time to first byte. Near 1 is healthy; near total/TTFT means a hop buffers. Plus streams ending at a round number of seconds.
  • Bounded by: a held stream → proxy_buffering off per route plus a canary that fails on first-byte ratio; a cut stream → every idle and total timeout above the longest gap, a heartbeat comment inside the shortest one, and a client resume.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A proxy either holds the upstream response or passes it on chunk by chunk. Holding is nginx's default and protects backend workers from slow clients. For a token stream it makes time to first token equal total generation time, with no error anywhere. So stream routes turn buffering and compression off, every hop's idle and total timeout sits above the longest gap, and you prove it with curl -N from outside the edge.

Q · Mechanism — Why doesn't a small buffer at least send the first tokens early? Because a size-triggered flush needs the size. With buffering on, nginx reads into buffers of one memory page (proxy_buffer_size and proxy_buffers, 4 or 8 KB each) and passes data on in buffer-sized pieces. A ten-token SSE stream is a few hundred bytes, so it never fills one and leaves when the origin closes. The Break it shows it: the 8 KB threshold proxy delivered its first event at the same 2 s as the full buffer. Large downloads flush early; small streams never do.

Q · Trade-off — Turn buffering off everywhere, or per route? Per route. With buffering off, the backend writes at the client's pace, so a slow phone holds a backend connection and its worker for the whole download. Async backends absorb that cheaply; thread-per-request ones run out of workers. Keep buffering on for documents and downloads, off for text/event-stream and long-poll routes. The tipping point is the response's shape: a stream needs every byte on time, a document only needs the last one.

Q · Failure — Streams die at exactly 15 s behind a new mesh, and nginx is already fixed. What's happening? Envoy's route timeout defaults to 15 s and spans until the upstream response is completely processed, so any stream longer than 15 s is cut while it's still flowing. It looks like 200 with a truncated body, or an Envoy 504 if headers hadn't gone out. Confirm with Envoy's access-log response flags (UT, upstream timeout) and a duration histogram that piles up at 15 s. Fix: timeout: 0s plus an explicit idle_timeout on stream routes only.

Q · Design — Browser to model through CDN, ALB, nginx and app: where does each setting go? The binding constraint is the shortest silence-tolerant hop. The CDN: no caching, buffering off, response timeout above the longest gap. The ALB: idle timeout above the longest gap, since it doesn't buffer. nginx: a separate stream location with buffering and gzip off. The app: flush per event and send a comment heartbeat. The signal to watch first is the client-measured first-byte ratio per hop. The decision record is which transport carries the agent's stream.

Pitfalls

  • Not the same: a buffered stream vs a cut stream
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "streaming is broken" with a 200 status and no error log.
    ↳ Difference: buffering delays the first byte and delivers everything at the end; a timeout delivers the start on time and then stops at a round number of seconds.
    ↳ Think instead: first byte late → a hop buffers; end early → a hop's timeout. They need opposite fixes.
  • "The model is slow"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the user's wait looks exactly like slow generation.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the origin's own time to first byte is unchanged; only the client's moved. The bytes left the origin on time and sat in a hop.
    ↳ Think instead: compare client and origin first-byte times before touching the model.
  • Don't turn buffering off globally.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: one line in http {} fixes the stream.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every download now runs at the client's pace on a backend worker, and slow clients exhaust a thread-per-request backend.
    ↳ Do instead: a separate stream location, or X-Accel-Buffering: no from the origin on stream responses only.
  • "Envoy streams by default, so a mesh path is safe"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: Envoy doesn't buffer responses, and its buffer filter only holds requests.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: its default route timeout of 15 s runs until the response completes, so long streams are cut instead of held.
    ↳ Think instead: "doesn't buffer" isn't "doesn't time out": check total and idle timeouts on every hop.
  • Don't test the stream against the app server.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: curl localhost:8000 is quick and it streams.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the bug lives in a hop you skipped; the test passes while users wait. curl without -N also buffers its own output.
    ↳ Do instead: curl -N from outside the edge, then hop by hop inward until the gap appears.
  • Shelf life: the buffer-or-forward choice is permanent. Product defaults move: nginx changed its upstream HTTP version in Mar 2026, and CDNs add per-route switches. Re-check every 3 months.
